An unknown set is stale. SECRETS and SECURITY are always stale on a product change. Gates that rely on a content-only signal are not selective. (2) The build and test run once per commit through `control-plane/agents/scripts/build-record.sh`, recorded by commit hash under `.agents/local/builds`; reviewers and the verifier read the record. The verifier's own independent re-run (A107) is unchanged. (3) `agent.sh plan-section` prints one section of PLAN.md. (4) task-author and intent-grill run in the main interactive session. (5) `agent.sh digest` prints a short run summary, and every stage transition says in one line that a context reset is safe (`/proofline resume ID`). Why: TASK-001 measured 146M Claude tokens; the lead used 210 turns and 45M tokens, the grill 15.7M; the run did 63 builds, 92 test runs and 24 `npm ci`; PLAN.md (49K characters) was read 23 times; the dependency security review ran 3 times without a `package.json` change. Rejected: a vector or memory store; skipping a gate on a guess (an unknown file set is stale). Known limit: the build-record key covers source only, not the node version or installed packages. Known limit: selective reuse uses the whole task-owned manifest, not a per-focus list.

- **A149. 0.0.7, learning: a lesson only from evidence and only with approval.** What: (1) Lessons: `lessons.sh` derives candidates from run evidence, writes them to `docs/wiki/lessons/observations.md` (each with a source gate or finding id; a sourceless candidate is rejected), validates them and counts repeats by script across runs. The lead proposes promotion at the second repeat (third run). Promotion into `AGENTS.md` `## Project rules` needs a `rule:<ID>` approval. (2) `agent.sh calibrate` prints config suggestions from metrics and plans; it never edits a file. (3) Friction report: `friction.sh` builds an anonymous, scrubbed report at run end; `friction send` files a GitHub issue only with a `report` approval bound to the report hash. Why: a lesson that nobody can trace to evidence, or that changes rules unasked, cannot be trusted. Rejected: a new memory store or vector DB; a self-modifying skill; automatic promotion; sending a report without approval; personal or team information in a report. Known limit: promotion goes only into `AGENTS.md`, not into config. Known limit: FAILED and BLOCKED runs cannot take the `rule` approval, so their candidates stay observations. Known limit: hook timeouts are not recorded in the ledger, so the report counts failovers and dispatch timeouts. Known limit: the end-to-end call from `metrics_run` is not covered by the lifecycle fixtures. Amended in 0.0.8 (A150): proposed at the second run.

- **A150. 0.0.8 patch.** What: (1) `knowledge <TASK>` is added to the entry skill (argument-hint, table) and to `proofline help`; the help/entry test now also compares the lead skill Commands table. (2) Lesson promotion is proposed at the second run (repeats>=1); this amends A149. (3) visual-proof `focus_order` false alarms (see A147): cause 1, the tabbables list included links in closed `<details>`, which a real Tab never reaches; the filter is limited to `details:not([open]) > :not(summary)`. Cause 2, `scrollIntoView`/`focus()` on the checked elements moved the sequential-focus start mid-page, so the first Tab started late (matters only with more than 40 tab stops). The fix skips the closed content and resets the focus start to `body`. On a built copy of a real site, `focus_order` fail rows went 724 -> 0 and `overlapping_interactive` 652 -> 0 (the 840 figure of A147 was not reproduced exactly). Why: the entry point gap was found after 0.0.7; the user wanted earlier promotion; a real run had 858 blocking rows. Rejected: loosening the `focus_order` rule; skipping the check for pages with `<details>`. Known limit: only the unit test covers cause 1; cause 2 was confirmed on a real site run, not in a test; the repro used `file:` URLs and its own config.

- **A151. 0.0.9, one-command delivery.** What: `deliver` prepares (knowledge first if not done; `agent.sh deliver-plan` writes SUMMARY.md with changed/knowledge paths, commit message, branch, PR kind/body, when merge and cleanup happen, open `rule:*` requests listed separately) and asks once; "approve delivery" is recorded as separate approvals for commit, push, pr, merge, cleanup, each bound to the content fingerprint and the summary sha256; `deliver-step` re-checks content/branch/message/body/HEAD and the step's approval before printing the commands the lead runs (agent.sh never commits/pushes/merges itself); FAILED run => draft PR, no merge step, cleanup after the PR is open; normal PR => `gh pr checks --watch` then `proofline merge`, cleanup only when MERGED; `rule:*` promotions are not covered by the delivery approval. Why: delivery took many separate prompts. Rejected: a blind single approval (not bound to shown content); cleanup before the PR/merge (loses the evidence the draft body and a failed merge report need). Known limit: a rule promotion changes AGENTS.md so the summary must be prepared and approved again. Known limit: if the summary output is piped into an early-closing reader, agent.sh can die holding its lock. Known limit: the real gh/push path is untested. Known limit: the commit trailer of the 0.0.9 delivery commits names Opus.
- **A152. 0.0.10, reopen a FAILED or BLOCKED run; no draft PR.** What: (1) `deliver-plan`/`deliver` refuse a FAILED or BLOCKED run in one line, `to reopen: /proofline reopen <ID>`; the draft pull request of A151 (`draft-pr-body`, the draft summary kind, the no-run `cleanup` approval) is removed, CODE_DONE is the only delivery path. (2) `/proofline reopen <ID>` (entry skill, lead Commands table, `proofline help`) runs `agent.sh reopen <ID>` (lead-only, reason on stdin): it needs the user's `reopen:<ID>` approval (bound to the PLAN.md hash, named for that run, recorded by the prompt hook like every approval; `approve` stays denied to every model), checks the plan freeze, the task contract and the scope again (files changed outside the frozen scope refuse the reopen), restores the execution state the run had before `terminate`, writes a `REOPEN` gate record marked `reopened_from` and a ledger row, and restarts the knowledge step. Gate records are not discarded: those that passed on unchanged inputs stay, a failed, BLOCKED or never-concluded gate and one whose inputs changed run again (`reuse` mode of 0.0.6); the fix-round allowance (limit stays `review.max_fix_rounds`) restarts at the reopen. A mutation-budget decision the plan needs (criteria above the budget) is asked first, before anything else is checked, and `reopen` applies the approved `raise-budget` itself. (3) The content fingerprint excludes `.agents/` (except the files a run's plan scope names: task-owned product content stays in), so a change confined to the control plane (`proofline upgrade` included) no longer makes a gate stale; only product files count. (4) `deliver-plan` on a CODE_DONE run whose knowledge step, report or DONE is missing prints what is left (exit 0, nothing written, no question) instead of `knowledge step not complete`; the lead runs those steps and asks once, and the one summary lists the knowledge-changed paths. The fingerprint and summary-sha256 binding of the approvals is unchanged. Why: a real run (TASK-001) ended FAILED on a test gate BLOCKED by the budget and a visual false alarm (fixed in 0.0.5/0.0.8), and nothing could take it to DONE. Rejected: delivering a FAILED run with a draft PR (it ships evidence of a failure as a deliverable, and leaves the run FAILED); the agent reopening on its own (a failed run is the user's decision: the approval is bound to the plan, recorded from the user's reply, and no model can create it); reusing `amend` (CODE_DONE only, discards every gate record, resets nothing for a terminated run); a new fingerprint scope that lists control-plane files one by one (drifts with every new control-plane file). Known limits: after a reopen a gate that had failed reads stale and runs again before any fix round starts; the commit approval no longer binds changes under `.agents/` (a commit still contains them; the pre-commit hook and the summary list them); a terminate reason is not re-checked on reopen (the user's approval is the check); `reopen` after a cleanup is impossible (the run is gone); deliver does not run the knowledge step itself, the lead does, before the summary and the one question; the real gh/push path is still untested.
- **A153. 0.0.11, scope discipline, observations, shortcut debt.** What: (1) The proof-review `plan` focus fails a hunk inside the plan scope that changes behaviour and ties to no acceptance criterion: an `unrequested` record with `"blocking": true` (schema, `validate-findings.mjs`, `gate.mjs` fail on it; the result row is `blocking`, `PLAN-CHECK.md` section 2 defines the test). A hunk that does not change behaviour (formatting, comments, import order) stays an informational `unrequested` record, and when the reviewer is unsure the hunk is informational; a path outside the scope stays informational as before (the lead's scope enforcement handles it). `blocking` is only valid inside a run. (2) The implementer report may carry an `## Observations` section (`file:line` and one sentence per issue seen but untouched because out of scope). The knowledge step shows them to the user as proposed new tasks; for each one the user approves, the task author writes a task into `tasks.dir`; nothing is written without the approval, and the implementer never fixes an observation. (3) A deliberate shortcut is marked in code with a comment `shortcut: <limit>, <when to improve>`. `agent.sh debt` (`debt.sh`, grep, no model; `proofline debt` and `/proofline debt`) lists them with `file:line`, limit and improvement condition, read-only and without a run; `agent.sh debt page` (lead, knowledge step) rewrites the one wiki page `docs/wiki/concepts/shortcut-debt.md` from the same list, so a removed shortcut drops off it, and writes nothing when the project keeps no wiki. (4) The implementer role gets a "check first" order: needed, already in the codebase, in the standard library, in an installed dependency, otherwise the minimum code. (5) Documentation rule: a new user-visible command, option or rule updates `proofline help`, the entry skill, the lead Commands table, the README and the relevant `docs/concepts` page before merge (CONTRIBUTING); the README has a command list for the first time (`reopen`, `knowledge` and `debt` included), and the CLI test compares it with `proofline help`. Why: a plan review that only listed unrequested changes let behaviour changes nobody asked for through; a corner cut on purpose was invisible after the run; a useful finding outside the task had nowhere to go but the implementer's urge to fix it. Rejected: blocking every unrelated change inside the scope (formatting, comments and import order are noise, and the reviewer cannot always judge; the rule would fail runs on style); making the external tool that inspired the check-first order and the shortcut comment a dependency (proofline is installable alone and names no third-party project, D33; both rules are written here instead); a model-written debt page (a script finds the comments, so the page cannot invent or miss one); letting the implementer file observations as tasks itself (a task is the user's decision, and the implementer owns no task folder). Known limits: a shortcut comment is only found with the `shortcut:` marker after a comment character, in files outside Markdown, `.agents/`, `.claude/` and `docs/wiki/`; the limit/condition split is the first `, ` or `; ` of the text; whether a hunk "changes behaviour" is the reviewer's judgement, the script only enforces the `blocking` mark; observations are model-reported and not counted by any gate.
- **A154. 0.0.12, installed files are control plane; one reopen question; the Stop hook supplies missing identifiers.** What: (1) A file `proofline init/upgrade` installs outside `.agents/` is control plane like `.agents/` itself (A152): the files `.agents/.proofline-manifest` lists outside `.agents/` (agent definitions, the entry skill), the patterns `.claude/agents/proofline-*.md` and `.codex/agents/proofline-*.toml`, and the marked proofline block of `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`. `content_fingerprint` leaves them out (the block is cut from the two files before the tree is written), so a gate does not go stale; `verify_scope` lists them apart ("installed proofline files changed") instead of failing, which is what lets `reopen` pass after an upgrade. For `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` a change is control plane only when the file outside the block equals HEAD; any edit outside the block (`## Project rules`) is a product change. A path a plan scope names stays tracked and counts in full (A152). The changed-path list that feeds the review tier skips them too, so an upgrade never raises the tier. (2) `reopen` checks freshness and scope first, then asks ONE question: when PLAN `## Tests` has more criteria than the budget, both requests (`mutation_budget`, `reopen:<ID>`) are written with `joint: reopen:<ID>` and one summary ("Raise the budget to N and reopen the run <ID>?") is printed; `approve` judges a request with that field by the kind words of the reopen, so the user's one reply ("I approve the reopen of <ID>") records both approvals. Approvals are still created only by `approve` from the user's own captured prompt (the prompt hook); `approve` stays denied to every model; each approval is single-use and bound to the PLAN.md hash as before. A budget approval or reopen approval that already exists is not asked again; only one missing: the plain single request. (3) The Stop hook no longer blocks (no rewrite loop). A Stop hook cannot edit the assistant's message in either runtime, so when `report-tokens` names an identifier the last message lacks, the hook emits a `systemMessage` with the matching lines of `agent.sh summary` (verbatim, untranslated), shown to the user next to the report. Rejected: a baseline hash change (RUN.yaml format; runs started before 0.0.12 keep working through the HEAD comparison); treating the whole `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` as control plane (hides the project's own rules edits); one combined approval kind (a second kind to bind, consume and document); a hook that rewrites the report (not possible); keeping the block and a longer skill rule (already failed, A44). Known limits: `.claude/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json`, `.codex/config.toml` and `.gitignore` are merged files that mix project and proofline keys; they stay product files. For `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` of a run started before 0.0.12 the baseline holds the whole-file hash, so the block-only change is recognised only against HEAD (an uncommitted or untracked file outside the block is judged as before). The appended identifier lines are a system message, not part of the model's text, and a runtime that ignores `systemMessage` on Stop shows nothing; the check is presence only (A44).

(2) `reopen` reuses a standing request only through `pending_request`: the latest request of the kind counts only while no approval of that kind is numbered above it, so a used request (approved, consumed) is never reused even when the PLAN hash is unchanged; a still pending unused request stays reusable, which keeps the joint question of A154 one question. (3) Process killing: the role rules (`control-plane/AGENTS.md`, every `roles/*.md` Does/Must-not table, lead skill hard rule 12) say that an agent stops only a process it started itself, by its own PID. The PreToolUse hook (`kill_guard` in `adapters/claude/hooks/proofline-hook.sh`, beside the merge guard, for every caller, with or without a run, installed or not) denies `pkill`, `killall`, `killall5`, `skill`, `slay`, `fuser -k`, `kill -1`, a PID operand `0` (`kill 0`, `kill -TERM 0`), `kill` whose PIDs come from a `$(...)` or backtick substitution that runs `pgrep`, `pidof`, `ps`, `lsof`, `fuser` or `pkill`, and a pipe from one of those into `xargs kill`; signal 0 (`kill -0`, `-s 0`) passes. It reads the scan's command records, so a path (`/usr/bin/pkill`), quotes (`p""kill`), a backslash, `sudo`/`env`/`command`/`xargs`/`busybox` wrappers and `sh -c "..."` are seen; `kill <pid>`, `kill $!`, `kill $PID` and `kill $(cat pidfile)` pass. The hook receives only the agent's own tool calls: a command the user runs with `!` in the terminal does not go through PreToolUse and is not affected. Why: an upgrade that creates `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` for the first time (only the block) staled the plan of a run although no product file changed; after an accepted move every later check recomputed the range from the old base and the record still named it; a kill by pattern (`pkill`, `killall`) can stop processes the agent never started, among them the user's own. (h) `content_fingerprint` now leaves out an `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` that is only the block (as if missing), so creating it by an upgrade does not change the fingerprint; a run whose gates were fingerprinted while such a file already existed (stripped to an empty file before 0.0.14) reads stale once after the upgrade to 0.0.14; (i) the kill guard reads the scan records: a substitution is seen as a bare `$` argument followed by the substituted command, so only the command right after `kill` counts, and `kill` text inside quoted strings, heredoc bodies and commit or PR bodies is ignored; `kill -0`, `-s 0` and `-n 0` (liveness probes) pass; `kill -TERM 0`, `kill -- 0` and `-1` anywhere are denied; `pkill`, `killall` without arguments or with `--help`/`-h`/`--version`/`-V` pass.

The outcome is read from records only: `merged.tsv` has the task (merged), run state FAILED or BLOCKED, an open question or an unanswered approval request (parked, reason `question`, first question line), otherwise parked "session ended without a result". Usage-limit text moves the same task to the next runtime (`batch.runtimes`; default `runtime.lead`, then the other CLI when installed), all runtimes exhausted or an authentication failure stops the batch with the task pending. After every task the worktrees the session added are removed and the checkout returns to the canonical branch; a dirty tree stops the batch. - **A160. 0.0.18, night mode closes its own processes, runs Codex sandboxed and checks the CI of the merge commit; SEO measures analytics by behaviour and robots.txt per bot (amends A157, A158; issues #135, #137).** What: (1) *Per-task timeout.* `batch.task_timeout` (minutes, default 120, validated by config-check, shown in SUMMARY.md and so in the approval hash) bounds one headless session. On expiry the session's process group is closed, the task is parked with the reason `timeout`, tasks that depend on it are skipped and the batch continues. (2) *Own process group.* `batch.sh` starts each session as the leader of its own process group (`set -m` around the background start; where a shell cannot do job control, for example dash without a terminal, `setsid` when it exists; the leader writes its own pid and pgid and the driver signals the group only when both equal the pid it started), and when the task ends (exit, error or timeout) signals that group (TERM, a short grace, KILL). It never signals pgid 0 or 1, its own group, or a group it did not verify; without a verified group it signals only the session pid. No `pkill`, `killall`, `pgrep`, `kill 0` or `kill -1`. A156 stays: agents are still forbidden to kill by name or pattern and the hook's guard concerns an agent's own Bash tool calls; the driver is a program the user starts (a terminal, or `proofline batch run`), so a `kill -TERM -<pgid>` inside it needs no exception, and the driver must not be launched from an agent tool call. (3) *Codex sandbox.* Night sessions run `codex exec -s workspace-write -c sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true` (the project folder is writable, package installs reach the network; the override lives in one variable in `batch.sh`). `danger-full-access` only when `agent.sh batch-plan <IDs> --codex-danger-full-access` was given: SUMMARY.md then carries `codex sandbox: danger-full-access` and a WARNING line, the approval is bound to that text, and the driver reads the choice from the approved SUMMARY.md only, never from config or environment. (4) *CI of the merge.* After a task merges the driver reads the merge commit SHA (`gh pr view <PR> --json mergeCommit`), pulls with `--ff-only` and waits for the CI runs of that SHA (`gh run list --commit <sha>`): any run red stops the batch ("main CI is red"), still running polls up to `batch.ci_wait_minutes`, and no run within the new `batch.ci_appear_minutes` (default 10) stops it ("no CI run appeared for <sha7>"). A candidate found by name only, a lone `dataLayer` and a same-origin `pixel-art.js` are information (`analytics_detected`, an info row); other third-party requests are listed as `third_party_requests`. (6) *robots.txt per RFC 9309.* For Googlebot and Bingbot the groups with the bot's token (case-insensitive, equal tokens combined) apply, else `*`; longest path wins, Allow wins a tie, `*` and `$` wildcards, empty Disallow allows all; every published page and sitemap page is tested and a page blocked for some bots is a `seo_robots` failure naming the bot. A page blocked for EVERY tested bot is skipped as `not_applicable` (reason `robots`, the detail names the bots), as in 0.0.16 ("only for pages not blocked by robots"); a blocked sitemap page still fails. (5b) The site's own deployed origin (`seo.site_url`) is first party (`siteRef` decides before the probe's `third_party` flag), and an initiator equal to the document URL (what a parser-initiated stylesheet or font reports) never counts, so a path such as `/stats/` cannot make a third-party stylesheet analytics. The driver reads the Codex sandbox from the approved SUMMARY.md once, right after `batch-check`, and passes it to its sessions, so a session cannot edit the file to widen later sessions. Limits: the Codex network override is the documented `sandbox_workspace_write.network_access` key, not run end to end here; on a system with neither job control nor `setsid` only the session pid is signalled; the markdown adapter and real sessions with fakes only stay as in A157; an initiator is known only when the browser reports it; only Googlebot and Bingbot are tested; a page blocked for every tested bot is skipped (`not_applicable`, reason `robots`) and not reported, so a robots-blocked page that was meant to stay private is not listed; only a page blocked for some bots, or one listed in the sitemap, is reported and the user may waive it. robots.txt rules that differ only by percent-encoding are not matched (false negative), and `Disallow: /dir/index.html` is not matched against a page collapsed to `/dir/` (false negative).

The driver tries `set -m`, then `setsid`, then a perl `setpgid` one-liner (perl ships with macOS), then python3 `os.setpgid`, and uses the first method whose probe process reports pgid equal to pid; the session checks the same itself and exits 125 otherwise. When no method works the batch is refused with one line (`batch: no way to start a headless session in its own process group on this machine ...`) and no session is started: the 0.0.18 pid-only fallback is removed, because a hung session could not be closed with its children (checked: signalling only the session pid left 3 of 3 descendants alive; every group method left 0 of 5). `PROOFLINE_TEST=1` with `PROOFLINE_BATCH_PGMETHOD` forces each method so every fallback is tested on every machine. (2) *Codex night profile.* Sessions no longer use the legacy `-s workspace-write`. Verified with `codex sandbox` (codex-cli 0.163.0) and the documented "Protected paths in writable roots": that mode keeps `.git`, `.agents` and `.codex` read-only, so a session could not branch, commit, add a worktree or write its run records, and the legacy `network_access` key does not apply to the profile. Sessions run in the named permissions profile `proofline_night`, passed as `-c default_permissions="proofline_night"`, `-c permissions.proofline_night.network.enabled=true` and `-c permissions.proofline_night.filesystem={...}`: read everywhere, write the project folder including `.git` and `.agents`, `.git/hooks`, `.git/config` and `.codex` read-only (a planted hook or `core.hooksPath` would run outside the sandbox), write `$TMPDIR`, network on. Verified inside the profile: `curl` to registry.npmjs.org returns 200; `git commit`, `branch`, `checkout -b` and `worktree add` inside the workspace succeed; `.agents/runs` is writable; `$HOME` is not. Package managers wrote caches under `$HOME`, which the profile keeps read-only: `npm view left-pad version` failed with EPERM on `~/.npm/_cacache` (curl worked), so "network on for package installs" was true only for tools that need no `$HOME` cache. The driver therefore passes `-c shell_environment_policy.set={...}` that points the caches into the writable temp dir (`$TMPDIR/proofline-pkg-<uid>`): `npm_config_cache`, `npm_config_store_dir`, `YARN_CACHE_FOLDER`, `YARN_GLOBAL_FOLDER`, `PIP_CACHE_DIR`, `GOCACHE`, `GOPATH`. Verified inside `codex sandbox -P proofline_night` with real commands: `npm view` and `npm install left-pad`, `pnpm add` (pnpm 10.33.2), `yarn add` (yarn 4.10.2), `pip3 download six`, `go get` and `go build` (uuid v1.6.0); `$HOME` stays read-only. Not verified, so not claimed: cargo, other package managers, a corepack download of an uncached version (`COREPACK_HOME` is not set, since redirecting it made the pnpm shim resolve another version). Rejected: making `~/.npm` and the other cache folders writable (opens `$HOME` for every tool). `codex exec` accepts the profile (it reaches the API and stops at the missing credentials; no model session ran). `--codex-danger-full-access` is unchanged, and the summary line starts `codex sandbox: proofline_night profile (`; `danger-full-access` keeps `codex sandbox: danger-full-access`. Git stays in the Codex session. The profile was verified only on codex-cli 0.163.0. `batch-plan` records `codex version:` in the summary when a Codex runtime can run, and the driver refuses a Codex runtime below 0.163.0 or with an unparsable `codex --version` (an error when the lead or `batch.runtimes` names it, left out with one line when it is only the installed fallback), instead of running an unknown sandbox. (3) *Nesting warning.* Seatbelt cannot nest on macOS (`sandbox-exec: sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted`), so a sandboxed Codex lead cannot start sandboxed `codex exec` workers. `batch-plan` therefore writes one WARNING line into SUMMARY.md (bound by the approval hash) when a Codex session can run as the lead (`runtime.lead`, `batch.runtimes`, or the installed fallback runtime tried when the first hits its usage limit; the same `rt_list` the driver uses), the plan was made without `--codex-danger-full-access` and at least one role resolves to codex; it names the roles and the two ways out: claude workers and reviewers (`proofline init --worker claude --reviewers claude`, no `--role ROLE=codex`), or planning again with `--codex-danger-full-access`. It is a warning, not a block. (4) *Session records.* Each session writes `.agents/local/batch/sessions/<ID>.<n>.rec` (key=value: id, n, runtime, method, log, start, then end, exit, timeout); `batch status` has a sessions section (task, #, runtime, start, end, exit, park reason, log; `124 (timeout)`; `no end recorded`), so a first real run can be diagnosed from records; a state without `sessions/` prints no section; `batch-plan` moves `sessions` into history with the other files. (5) *Markdown-only adapter, by design.* `batch-plan` refuses a non-markdown `tasks.adapter` (exit 1, nothing written) with the next step: set `tasks.adapter` to markdown, import each task with `/proofline task <issue reference>`, run `/proofline batch <ID...>` again. Reasons: `depends_on` and `Suggested class` live in the task file's own front matter and sections, and github, jira and linear resolve ids through network calls that an unattended driver must not depend on at night. (6) *Kill guard (#127).* The `proofline-hook.sh` scanner emits two more record kinds, the run path of a literal command word and here-document bodies; it skips `#` comments and `case` labels, treats `$((...))` as one word, ends `< <(cmd)` correctly, and strips leading tabs from the delimiter only for `<<-`. `kill_guard` now also denies: PID operands `0` or `-1` in any spelling (`00`, `+0`, `$((0))`); PIDs from `pgrep`, `pidof`, `ps`, `lsof`, `fuser`, `netstat`, `ss`, `pstree` or `jps` that reach `kill` through a variable, a `for` or `read` loop, `mapfile` or `$@` in the same command; `find -exec kill|pkill` and `find | xargs kill`; `eval` and a variable command word whose value the same command assigns; `setsid`, `su -c`, `flock` and similar wrappers; interpreter one-liners, here-documents and piped text (`python -c`, `perl -e`, `node -e`, `ruby -e`, `php -r`, `lua -e`, `awk` (only where it can run a command: `system(`, a pipe to or from a command, a coprocess), `osascript -e`) containing `pkill`, `killall`, `slay`, `fuser -k`, `os.kill`/`process.kill`/`Process.kill` with 0 or -1, `killpg(getpgrp())`, psutil loops that kill, or string literals that are such command lines; the unquoted here-document body is scanned for `$(...)` and backticks because the shell executes them; and the content of script files the command runs (`sh|bash x`, `./x`, `source x`, `python|node|perl|ruby x`) or writes in the same command, when the file is a text file of at most 256 KB under the project (not `node_modules` or `.git`) or a temp dir. `kill -TERM "-$pgid"` is no longer mistaken for `xargs kill`. Decision, tripwire not boundary: the guard stops an agent's honest mistake (killing a user's processes by name); it is not a security boundary against a hostile agent, whose boundary is the runtime's permission mode and sandbox. What stays unseen, and why each is decided: a payload assembled at run time from data the hook cannot see (`$(curl ...)`, a decoded string, a variable assigned in an earlier tool call), because nothing is there to read and a rule over arbitrary `$VAR` or `eval "$x"` would deny `eval "$(brew shellenv)"`; a script another tool call writes and a later call runs from outside the project and temp dirs, a file over 256 KB, a binary, a symlink, and `node_modules` code, because third-party code legitimately contains `kill` text and reading arbitrary paths would mean scanning system files; a PID taken from a search in an earlier command (`pgrep x > f`, then `kill $(cat f)`), because `kill $(cat pidfile)` is the normal way to stop what the agent started; a variable command word assigned in an earlier call; `kill -- -$PGID` and `process.kill(-child.pid)`, which stay allowed because killing a group by number is how an agent stops the tree of its own detached child (only literal 0 and -1 and a group from `getpgrp()` are denied); and interpreter code that only prints these words, which is denied because text and an exec target cannot be told apart; the denial text now says exactly that and that the user can run the command with the `!` prefix. Also unseen, each with its reason: another tool's text (`npm run`, `make` and package.json scripts), because the commands inside are text that the hook never sees and resolving them means running or parsing that tool; remote or container targets (`ssh host pkill x`, `docker exec c pkill x`), because they signal processes on another machine or in a container, not the user's local processes, denying them would stop legitimate remote administration, and the user's own machine is what the rule protects; the part of a single here-document body beyond 200000 characters, which the scanner truncates and treats as unreadable; and a relative script path that cannot be resolved (`cd` to a non-literal directory, or a script calling another by a path relative to its own directory), while `cd dir &&` with a literal directory is resolved. Env records: a `NAME=` argument is not an environment assignment, only a prefix before the command word is, so `ps -o pid=` no longer breaks the pending-substitution and variable taint logic. Also denied: `xargs pkill`, taint through arrays and `< <(pgrep x)` read loops, `cat x.sh | sh`, and scripts after `cd dir &&`; long shell options (`--norc`) are parsed correctly. Interpreter rules are restricted to kill-by-name verbs, pid 0 and -1, `getpgrp` group kills, psutil `process_iter` loops that kill, code that kills what `pgrep`, `pidof` or `lsof` returned, and `os.system` or exec of those verbs; a kill of a pid the code spawned itself (`child.pid`, a Popen handle) is not a kill fed by a search, and code that reads `/proc` or runs `ps -o rss= -p <pid>` is allowed. Cost: script text is read only when it holds `kill`, `slay` or `fuser` (or a variable command word). The guard has its own 20 s budget: past it, a command or text that holds a kill word is denied and everything else is allowed, because a command that cannot be read in time must not pass a kill. Before, the hook's 30 s timeout let the command through untouched, fail-open, per Claude Code's documented non-blocking hook timeout. The largest repo script (157 KB) measured 47.7 s before and 4.4 s after. (7) *Freshness and fingerprint (#128, #131, #132, #133).* #128: `unsupported_evidence_check` accepts a validator `BASE:` that is the run's base or a base before an accepted control-plane-only move, resolved through the run's `base-moved` ledger lines (`base_moved_predecessors`, at most 100 links); an unrelated base is still refused, and migration evidence has no `BASE:` line. #132: `control_plane_only` treats an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md that HEAD does not have yet (untracked or newly added) as control plane when the whole working-tree file is the proofline block, so `reopen`, `verify-scope` and the tier agree with the fingerprint; extra text keeps it a product change, and a file that exists in HEAD keeps the A154/A155 outside-the-block comparison. #133: `content_fingerprint legacy` computes the 0.0.12/0.0.13 value, and `gate_focus_status` accepts a gate record equal to it only when a block-only AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md exists; the two rules differ only in such a file, so every product byte stays bound, nothing is written, and records written since 0.0.14 never take this path. #131, design decision: a new AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md with project text besides the block, a symlink, or a file without markers stays a product change, because it is the instructions every agent reads and accepting appended text would let a control-plane commit carry project rules past the plan and the scope check; the stale-plan message and the scope check now name the file (`Changed outside the control plane: AGENTS.md (...)`) and the action (amend and refreeze, or move the text out and keep only the block). (8) *SEO (#137, #140).* robots.txt rule paths and page paths are compared in the same RFC 9309 percent-encoded normal form (`Disallow: /caf%C3%A9/` blocks `café/index.html`, `/a%20b` blocks `a b`, `%7e` equals `~`, hex case ignored, a lone `%` becomes `%25`). A page file `dir/index.html` is tested under the URL form it is published under: its sitemap `<loc>`, else its canonical, else both forms, and in the last case it counts as blocked only when both are blocked, so `Disallow: /dir/index.html` no longer fails a page published as `/dir/`. `siteRel` and `pageUrl` decode with a safe decoder (valid escapes decoded, a malformed `%` stays as written; `decodeURIComponent` threw), except `%2F`, `%25`, `%3F` and `%23`, which stay encoded, so `/a%2Fb` is not read as `/a/b` and `Disallow: /a/b` does not block it. (9) *Real Chrome.* `tests/skills/visual-proof-seo-browser.test.mjs` runs the real `measure.mjs` in Chrome against a local http server (the "third party" is the same server under the host name `localhost`; no network) and skips when `measure.mjs --detect` finds no browser. Observed: an inert `type="text/plain"` script is not requested and gives no consent item; an executable third-party script before consent fails; a first-party loader that calls `fetch` and adds a third-party script is attributed by its initiator; a parser-initiated third-party stylesheet under a `stats` path is not analytics; with `seo.site_url` set to the test origin nothing is third party. (10) *Missing sitemap.xml or robots.txt is information (`not_measured`), by design,* for three reasons: RFC 9309 defines a missing robots.txt as "everything may be crawled", so its absence is a valid state; a sitemap is optional; and with a `file:` or localhost base the measured folder is not the deployed host, so the deployed files cannot be proven absent and a blocking finding would have no evidence. A blocking finding was rejected (it would fail projects that deploy these files at build time) and a warning severity was rejected (the report has only pass, fail and not_measured). (11) *Image initiator, by design.* Chrome's DevTools protocol reports an `<img>` load made at parser time as `{type: parser, url: <document>}` and one made from a timer as `{type: other}`; neither names a script, and `Network.setAttachDebugStack` changes nothing. `fetch`, `sendBeacon` and dynamically added scripts do report the script. A tracking pixel is therefore attributed by its own URL and the project's candidate list only. Patching the page (wrapping `Image`) to learn the caller would alter the page being measured, which the measurement must not do, so the page is not patched. (12) *Only Googlebot and Bingbot are checked, by decision:* they are the bots the spec names; any other token would run through the same code path and is added by extending the list. Prefix tokens such as `googlebot-news` are different tokens under RFC 9309 (a group matches by the bot's own product token), so a `googlebot-news` group is not applied to Googlebot. Why: a night batch could leave a hung session's children running when no group method existed; Codex sessions could not commit or write run records under the legacy sandbox mode and had no network; the kill guard let an agent kill by name through variables, loops, interpreters and scripts; a valid run was refused after a base move, an uncommitted block-only AGENTS.md blocked `reopen`, gates recorded under the 0.0.12/0.0.13 rule read stale after an upgrade; robots rules written in percent-encoded form or against `index.html` were mismatched. Alternatives rejected: a pid-only mode when no group method works (a hung session's children would outlive it); committing in the driver instead of the Codex session (a large redesign that changes who commits); keeping legacy `workspace-write` (cannot write `.git`); denying every `kill $VAR` (an agent's own PID is normal) and every kill-like word in shell scripts (a shell script is parsed as commands, only interpreter code gets the text rules); negative literal PIDs other than `-1` (a group the code started itself); reading arbitrary paths in the hook; rewriting stored gate records (sealed); writing a ledger line from a read-only command; accepting any base on evidence; accepting two fingerprints without the block-only precondition; treating text beside the block as control plane; patching the page to find an image's initiator; a blocking or warning severity for a missing sitemap or robots.txt. Limits, each decided: `git push -u` pushes but cannot record the upstream because `.git/config` is read-only (the delivery step checks `refs/remotes`, so `push -u` is unchanged); a worktree outside the project and `/tmp` itself are not writable in the profile (proofline worktrees live under the project and `$TMPDIR` is writable); a Codex lead on macOS cannot dispatch sandboxed Codex workers because sandboxes cannot nest, and the choice between claude workers and `--codex-danger-full-access` stays with the user, surfaced by the WARNING, which also covers the installed fallback runtime; no real Codex model session ran, only `codex sandbox` and `codex exec` up to the credential check, so the first real run is the user's and a problem opens a new issue; an approval (commit, push, summary) bound to an old fingerprint is asked once more after such an upgrade; package installs in the Codex night profile are verified only for npm, pnpm, yarn, pip and go; the kill-guard unseen forms in (6).
- **A162. 0.0.20, shortcut comments and a README bound, a process-group timeout for command discovery, a `logging` focus, entry-point validation by design (amends A153, A161; related A78).** What: (1) *Shortcut comments.* Five comments carried a foreign shortcut label; they now read `shortcut: <limit>, <when to improve>` so `proofline debt` lists them. `tests/shared/check-static.sh` fails on a foreign label (the allowed tag list is one variable) and on a README above a bound in lines and in bytes; CI's static job and the self-tests run it. (2) *Discovery timeout.* `run_with_timeout` in `bin/lib/discover.sh` starts its command as a process-group leader with the same four methods as the night-mode driver (`set -m`, `setsid`, perl, python3), accepts a method only when a probe reports pgid equal to pid, and on timeout closes the group with TERM then KILL, never pgid 0, 1 or its own group, so a hung `sh -c` leaves no grandchildren. `nap`, `grp_alive` and `pg_start` are a copy of the driver's functions, kept identical by a drift test. When no method works the command is killed directly, documented as a shortcut comment. (3) *README.* Slimmed; night-mode and process-rule detail moved to `docs/concepts/night-mode.md`. (4) *Logging.* A deterministic `logging` focus opens in SECURITY when a line the diff adds is a log call (config `risk.log_sensitive.content`) and names a sensitive word (`risk.log_sensitive.words`: password, token, secret, authorization, cookie, email, phone, card, iban, ssn, tckn; both extensible), matched per added line, never per file. The focus only opens a review: the exploit-proof skill gets a `[log]` sink (request bodies, Authorization and Cookie headers, tokens, passwords, secret keys, personal data, CR/LF injection into plain-text logs) and a finding still needs a concrete path from a source to the log call. The implementer role uses the project's own logger and the standard written in AGENTS.md, and the AGENTS.md template carries no logging text (it is the whole hash-tracked proofline block); the project's own "Logging" section lives outside the block, where `upgrade` leaves it alone, and the `rules` focus checks it. The log-call pattern covers Console, Debug and Trace calls, `Fprint*` in any case, paren-less `print` and `puts`, `var_dump` and `dump`, so `json.dump(password)` also opens a review (the focus only opens a review and yields no finding); `config-check` refuses an invalid `risk.log_sensitive.content` expression and an empty or missing `words`, which silently fell back to a whole-file match. (5) *Entry-point validation, two tiers.* A `## Contracts` bullet of PLAN.md is a mandatory entry point only when it declares one (method plus path, endpoint, webhook, queue consumer, graphql mutation, rpc method, CLI flag or command, `validation.entry_words`), is not that entry point's own removal, is not marked unchanged or documented (`entry_skip`), and marks new or changed input (an `entry_input` word, or an `entry_new` word with no `entry_output` word). Such an entry point must carry one `## Validation` line: `accepts <what>; limits <limits>; rejected at <where, server side>`. `agent.sh freeze` and `refreeze` refuse a plan with a mandatory entry point and no complete line, and refuse a QA plan without an `[invalid-input]` scenario naming it; the plan-contract and qa-plan validators apply the same rules. Output-only and unchanged bullets, bare noun mentions and removals are excluded; a bullet that only mentions an entry word (`entry_candidates`) is information: `agent.sh pipeline` lists it as `validation.possible` and the freeze prints a note, nothing refuses. `agent.sh entry-tier "<bullet>"` prints `mandatory`, `information` or `none`, and the corpus `tests/fixtures/entry-points/corpus.tsv` (run by `tests/fixtures/entry-points/run-corpus.sh`, which prints precision and recall) pins the tiers. The expressions are the `validation.*` keys (`entry_words`, `entry_candidates`, `entry_input`, `entry_new`, `entry_output`, `entry_skip`, `code_patterns`); both validators carry the same defaults and read the project's `validation.*` keys themselves, and `config-check` validates the block. `validation.*` is read at freeze and refreeze and is not hash-bound; a refreeze of a run frozen before the rule re-validates the plan, so the amendment needs the `## Validation` line and the `[invalid-input]` scenario. Code patterns (`validation.code_patterns`) over scope files and the diff are information only. (6) *Legacy risk freeze.* The upgrade adds the default signal `risk.log_sensitive`, which `risk_sha256` binds. A freeze whose hash equals the hash of the block without that key stays valid, and that run keeps its frozen focus set with no `logging` focus; a run frozen under the new rule hashes the key, so editing it is refused. `proofline upgrade` therefore does not invalidate the freeze of runs in flight. (7) *Static rule.* The foreign-shortcut-label rule reads the whole comment part of a line (a leading `'` counts as a comment prefix only at line start, to avoid strings); a prose line that starts with `ponytail:` would also fail. Why: the foreign label was invisible to `proofline debt`; the old timeout killed only the direct child; a README that carries every detail is read by nobody; sensitive data in logs is a common leak and a word match on added lines is cheap and needs no model; validation of external input was left to reviewer attention and nothing asked the plan or the QA plan to say where input is rejected, and the one deterministic source before the freeze is PLAN.md; a single broad word list made ordinary contract bullets (`consumers: billing`, `The handler returns 404`) refuse the freeze and any removal word anywhere exempted a real entry point, hence two tiers; re-binding the risk hash on upgrade would silently accept any edit, hence the legacy rule. Rejected: a shared `pgroup.sh` (breaks "no file sharing", and `cli-test` sources `discover.sh` alone); refusing `init` when no group method exists (a trial run is not worth a failed `init`, so that case keeps the direct kill); a line bound alone for the README (paragraphs shrank, lines did not, so bytes are bound too); a new skill or role for logging; a new skill or role for validation; imposing proofline's own log standard (the project writes its own in AGENTS.md); matching the whole file for the logging focus (an edit near an old log call would open it); an LLM or semantic detector and an `UNSUPPORTED` result for logging (reading the code needs no tool); refusing on a code-pattern match (uncertain, would block ordinary plans); one broad entry word list with refusal, and a removal exemption on any removal word (see Why); re-binding `risk_sha256` on upgrade (it would accept any edit); keeping a logging example as a comment in the AGENTS.md template and telling users to ignore it (the template is the hash-tracked block); a risk-signal focus for validation (it would produce findings from word matches). Limits, each decided: a log word match alone is never a finding, because only a path from a source to the log call is evidence; the logging focus sees only lines the diff adds, because matching old code would open it for unrelated edits; an entry point not listed in `## Contracts` is not seen, because PLAN.md is the only deterministic source before the freeze and code patterns are uncertain; the validation check proves that a line and a scenario exist, not that the limits are right or enforced, because that is the review's and the QA's work; a bullet that only mentions an entry word is information and never refuses, because a false refusal blocks an ordinary plan while the missed case is still listed by `pipeline` and the freeze note, and the corpus bounds the tiers; the validators carry the `validation.*` defaults but read the project's keys themselves, because they run without the CLI and must agree with the freeze; a run frozen before this rule keeps its focus set without `logging`, because upgrade must not invalidate a freeze; the discovery timeout copy of the driver's group functions is kept identical by a test, because the files share nothing; with no group method the discovery timeout kills only the direct child, because failing `init` for a trial run costs more than a possible leftover process; the shortcut tag list covers the tags in use and a new tag is added to the one variable.
- **A163. 0.0.21, the task file moves in the delivery commit, a missing CI check is said early, and `approve batch` starts the night driver in the background (amends A157, A160, A161).** What: (1) *Task file.* With the markdown adapter the commit step of `deliver` runs `agent.sh task-source-done <ID>`, which moves the task file to `done/` (Status line `done`) before `git add -A`, so the move is part of the delivery commit; the recorded task path and the completion-report receipt follow the file. Other adapters and a file already in `done/` are left alone. The merge-step text says that on a failed merge the move exists only in the unmerged pull request branch. (2) *No CI.* `agent.sh ci-check` prints `ci: present (<file>)`, `ci: absent` plus the warning "no CI check runs on pull requests here. proofline merge does not merge a PR that has no checks.", or `ci: unknown` (not a GitHub repository). `doctor` warns, the delivery summary warns, `batch-plan` writes a BLOCKER into the summary and refuses the batch, and `agent.sh ci-task-command` prints one ready `/proofline task Add a GitHub Actions workflow ...` line with the project's own build and test commands. (3) *Background driver.* After the user's "approve batch" the lead runs `agent.sh batch-start` (lead only): it starts the driver detached from the session (own process group, SIGHUP ignored, stdin `/dev/null`, output to `.agents/local/batch/driver.log`, `driver.pid` holds pid and group), under a sleep inhibitor (`caffeinate -i -w <pid>` on macOS, `systemd-inhibit` on Linux, plainly "none available" otherwise), refuses a second start, and prints `driver started, pid N, log <path>`, the inhibitor line and `plug in the computer; do not close the laptop lid.` (the batch summary says that line once too, and the summary hash binds it). `agent.sh batch-stop` and `proofline batch stop` stop only the driver they recorded (verified group, TERM, grace, KILL) and park the running task with the reason `stopped`; `batch status` starts with a `driver:` line. `proofline batch run` in a terminal stays the same driver. (4) *Next step.* `next-user.sh` reads the batch folder for `batch`, `batch status` and `batch stop` (states ci, nobatch, unapproved, running, approved, stopped, finished-parked, finished-clean): no CI gives the ready CI task line, not approved `reply "approve batch" in this session to start the batch`, started `driver started, log: .agents/local/batch/driver.log. In the morning: /proofline batch status`, a parked task `/proofline resume <ID>, then reply in this session to the open question: ...` (or `reopen`, `deliver`, `run` by the run's state), none parked the next queued task, stop `/proofline batch status`; `deliver` for a run that is ready, and `--error=ci`, give the CI task line. Why: the done-move happened after the merge, in a second commit nobody made, so the task stayed in `todo/`; a project with no CI discovered at the merge step that nothing could ever be delivered, and a batch repeated that failure once per task; the night command needed a terminal the user had to open and keep after approving in the session, which a closed session or a sleeping Mac broke. Rejected: a setting that lets `proofline merge` merge without CI (the merge rule stays: no checks, no merge); a separate terminal command after the approval (one more step to forget, and the session already knows the approval is valid); stopping by process name or pattern (it can hit another user's or project's process; the kill guard of A156 denies it, and the recorded group is exact); a watchdog that restarts the driver (a crash loop would repeat a half-done task; the user resumes it); moving the task file in a separate commit after the merge (a second approval and a dirty main). Not verified: the real `caffeinate` and `systemd-inhibit` were only exercised with fakes that honour `-w` and run the command, so whether the machine stays awake with the lid open, and what the lid does, is not proven here (closing the lid sleeps most laptops whatever the inhibitor holds, hence the reminder); the background start was tested on the process-group methods available on the test machines, not on every OS; the CI check reads workflow files for a `pull_request` trigger and does not know whether a branch rule requires the checks. Limits: `ci: unknown` is not a block; a stopped driver's running task is parked `stopped` and resumed by hand.
- **A164. 0.0.22, CI under ten minutes, a working agreement and test policy, and the product evidence model with the `product-spec` skill (amends A76; related A109, A153).** What: (1) *CI.* macOS jobs, the browser measurement (`visual-browser`) and the benchmark report run only on `schedule` and `workflow_dispatch`; pushes to main and pull requests are Linux only. (2) *Template.* `tests/shared/fixture-lib.sh` builds one installed template per content hash of the control-plane files, and `test-lib.sh` and `cli-test` copy it per scenario; each scenario still owns its copy; a changed control-plane file gives a new hash and a rebuild. (3) *Units.* `sc_every_state` and `cli-test` are scenario units. (4) *Weights.* CI uploads per-unit seconds (`SELFTEST_TIMES_FILE`); `tests/selftest-weights.sh` rebuilds the weights file; an unlisted unit counts as the median. (5) *Affected tests.* `tests/affected.sh` maps changed files to suites through `tests/affected-map.txt`; it decides only what can be skipped, and an unmapped, shared or uncertain change runs the suite. (6) *Working agreement.* CONTRIBUTING holds the lead, review and agent-hygiene rules and the test policy (agents run only `tests/affected.sh`; the full self-test is CI's job). (7) *Product.* Claims are fact, assumption or decision; a fact needs a source (web: URL, access date, quote; interview: id, quote; data: query or script and output hash); `product-spec` writes the PRD, checks it deterministically, gates splitting, checks requirement coverage and traces a requirement to its task, test, evidence and pull request from records; the reviewer role has the focus `spec`; intent-grill batches up to three lettered questions and asks for anti-goals. Why: a main push took 36 minutes because nine macOS jobs shared five free slots, every scenario installed proofline again, the weights were stale and two units took about 500 seconds each; product work needs the same evidence discipline as code. Rejected: a new role for PRD review (the reviewer role takes a focus); a catalogue of product frameworks (one lean PRD, detail on request); personas without a source; showing numeric scores as if measured; macOS on every main push (nine jobs, five slots, no extra signal over the nightly run).
- **A165. 0.0.23, product discovery and assessment (amends A164).** What: (1) *Discovery.* The `product-discovery` skill and `/proofline product discover frame|research|interviews|competitors|opportunities <slug>` write `FRAME.md`, `RESEARCH.md`, `INTERVIEWS.md`, `COMPETITORS.md` and `OPPORTUNITIES.md` in `<product.dir>/<slug>/`, each gated by a read-only checker. Claims have ids (`C-n`, `INT-n`, `OP-n`, `S-n`); a number that is not a sourced fact is `unsourced-number`; a competitor cell is value, URL, observation date and quote, and is flagged `stale` after `product.stale_days` (default 90); every quote must occur verbatim in the raw interview text, which lives only under `.agents/local/product-discovery/` and is never tracked. (2) *Reference.* The fact source `ref <slug>#C-n` lets a PRD cite a claim by id; it is valid only when the claim is itself a valid fact. (3) *Assessment.* The `product-assess` skill and `/proofline product assess assumptions|probes|premortem|redteam|decision <slug>` write `ASSUMPTIONS.md`, `PROBES.md`, `PREMORTEM.md`, `REDTEAM.md` and `DECISION.md`: importance and evidence are `high|medium|low`; a probe's thresholds are locked by a timestamp and a sha256 before the result, and a changed threshold is rejected, also against the committed version; the red team is the reviewer with focus `strategy` on an independent agent, at most 2 rounds; the decision is `build|clarify|stop` with ADR sections. (4) *Stop gate.* `check-prd.mjs --ready` refuses the split under an effective `decision: stop`. (5) *Outcome.* `/proofline product outcome <slug>` records metric id, baseline, script and output hashes and the value; `check-outcome.mjs` rejects a value that does not match the output file, and a lesson candidate needs approval (A149). (6) `/proofline trace` also shows the evidence, assumption, decision and outcome links, and every new command ends with the user's next step (A159). Why: a PRD built on numbers nobody can open, personas nobody met and thresholds chosen after the result only looks evidence-based; each link now has an id, a source or a hash a script can check. Rejected: a persona without a source (an invented person is an assumption and is written as one); raw interviews in git (personal data, and history cannot be unpublished); numeric scores presented as measured (a 1-10 risk score looks measured and is not; only high, medium and low are allowed); setting thresholds after the result (the probe is locked by hash first, so a result cannot move its own success line); a new reviewer role for the red team (the existing role with a focus is enough).

- **A166. 0.0.24, visual proof of native apps with the project's own tools; ui-design platform rules (amends A82, A147; related A98, A102).** What: (1) *Native measurement.* `visual-proof` gets `scripts/native.mjs` and `references/NATIVE.md`: `--detect` decides the target (Flutter, Android, iOS, React Native, desktop) from files and finds the project's own UI or screenshot test tool and run command (`--run` proves it once); uiautomator and generic JSON output are measured for labels, touch target size (44pt iOS, 48dp Android), large text, dark theme and a screenshot with sha256 per spec state; checks the output cannot show are listed `not_measured`; no tool or device is `UNSUPPORTED` with one suggestion line. The report validator accepts the native sections; web measurement is unchanged. (2) *ui-design.* `references/NATIVE.md` holds the native mobile rules (touch targets, platform navigation, system text size, dark theme, safe areas); UI.md gets an optional `target` (default `web`); `keyboard` per screen is required for web and optional for native mobile targets. Why: A82 limited visual proof to a browser, so a native app could only be reviewed by reading code; projects that already run Flutter, Espresso or XCUITest tests produce structured output that can be measured without proofline owning a device farm. Rejected: proofline installing its own mobile test tool or driving a simulator (heavy, platform-specific, and the project's command already produces the output); passing when no tool exists (A98: an unmeasured check is UNSUPPORTED, never PASS). Not tested: real emulator or device runs.
- **A167. 0.0.25 patch: batch driver tests, README headroom, native output formats documented (amends A157, A160, A161 for the batch test; A164 for the README bound note).** What: (1) *Batch test flakiness.* `sc_driver_stop` and `sc_driver_crash` in `control-plane/agents/scripts/batch-test.sh` failed now and then. Root cause: the scenarios' EXIT trap ran `kill "$unrel"` without `|| :`, and under `set -e` a failed kill (the helper process was already reaped, a race) exited the scenario with status 1 after its `ok` line. The driver was unaffected. Fix: the guard `|| :` in `batch-test.sh`. Verified with 64 runs of each scenario before (`sc_driver_stop` 4 failures, `sc_driver_crash` 1 failure) and 96 runs of each after, under 16 parallel workers, with 0 failures. (2) *README headroom.* The README is slimmed from 12482 to 10895 bytes; the bound is unchanged (12500 bytes, 178 lines). The "Real output" section moved to `docs/concepts/workflow.md`. (3) *Native output formats.* The formats `visual-proof` measures for native apps are documented in `docs/concepts/testing.md`; no new parser. Why: a test that exits 1 after its ok line hides real failures behind noise, and the README was within 18 bytes of its bound. Rejected: raising the README bound (the bound exists to keep the first page short); sleeping longer in the tests (hides the race and slows every run); writing parsers for more tools (A166 measures the project's own tool output and the documented formats are enough). Confidence: high.
- **A168. Release version bump script `tests/ci/bump-version.sh` (dev tooling; amends the Versions rules of CONTRIBUTING).** What: the 0.0.25 release commit replaced "0.0.24" everywhere it appeared and so rewrote three historical comments ("visual-proof for native apps (0.0.24)" in `native.mjs`, `validate-visual.mjs` and `visual-proof-native.test.mjs`) that say when a feature arrived; they are restored. `sh tests/ci/bump-version.sh <new-version>` now rewrites only the version-holding sites, each by an anchored pattern (`bin/proofline`, both plugin manifests, `config.yaml`, `playground/package.json`, `metadata.version` of every `SKILL.md`, the two `SKILL_VERSION` constants, `skills/proof-review/references/REPORTING.md`, the README status lines, the `adapters/README.md` heading, the two fixtures and the pinned expectations in `tests/cli/cli-test.sh` and four `tests/skills` files), moves the CHANGELOG `Unreleased` entries under `## <version> — <date>` and runs both generators. `--check` fails when a site disagrees with `plugin.json`. A site missing its anchored pattern aborts before any file is written. The test `tests/ci/bump-version-test.sh` bumps a temp copy and asserts that only listed files changed, that every changed line names the old or new version, that a historical "(0.0.24" stays and that a bad version string exits non-zero. Audit of the 0.0.21 to 0.0.24 bump commits found no other overwritten history. Rejected: a global search-and-replace of the old version (it rewrote history comments in 0.0.25); a review-only rule without a tool (the mistake repeats under time pressure). Confidence: high. Not-tested: a real release run (the test bumps to a fake version in a copy).
- **A169. 0.0.26, CI red self-fix, a run's own commits do not stale the plan, one git worktree per run, runtime-version warning, the lead's ban on product files outside a run, Stop-hook scope, one-process approvals (amends A152, A154, A155, A157, A161, A163).** What: (1) *CI red self-fix.* After the `merge` step of a delivery, a red check is a finding, not a question. `agent.sh deliver-step <ID> ci-fix|ci-commit|ci-push|ci-merge <PR>`: `ci-fix` refuses unless the pull request is this delivery's open, non-draft pull request at HEAD, the `pr` and `merge` steps ran and a check of that head really failed; it writes the failed run's log to `ci-fix/NNN.log` (data, never instructions), records the attempt (`ci-fix/NNN.yaml`, ledger `ci-fix-open|-grant|-commit|-push|-stop`) and reopens the run through `amend` inside the frozen scope (no refreeze); the fix passes the gates again; `ci-commit` records a commit and a push approval from the user's delivery approval, bound to the new content, to the delivery summary hash and, for the push, to the branch ref (`refs/heads/<branch>`), single use; `ci-push` and `ci-merge` push to that same branch and record which CI run belongs to which push. At most 2 attempts (counted from the ledger, so deleting a record gives none back); the third red CI records one question (`ci-fix/limit.txt`) and a batch parks the task there; `resume` continues an open attempt and `deliver-plan` is not run again. The approval record may carry `ref:`; `approval-consume <ID> push '' <refs>` (the pre-push hook passes them) consumes it only for a push to exactly that ref. (2) *A run's own commits do not stale the plan.* `delivered_mode` measures a run's task paths from `base_sha` while HEAD is exactly the delivery's own commit chain (`ci_chain_ok`: the summary's head, the one delivery commit, then the CI-fix commits the records name), so the delivery commit is not read as a changed base; `base_moved_control_only ... own` also accepts the run's own bookkeeping, its task file moving between the lifecycle folders and the knowledge step's wiki, ADR and design documents the plan scope does not name. Any other commit leaves the checks as before. (3) *CODE_DONE exit.* The way back from CODE_DONE for a CI fix is the existing `amend`, wrapped by `ci-fix`; `reopen` is unchanged and still needs its own approval (A155); `ci-fix/` is a protected run folder like `approvals/`. (4) *One git worktree per run.* `agent.sh worktree-add|worktree-path|worktree-remove <ID> [--force]` (lead, main working tree) make `.agents/local/worktrees/<ID>`, detached at the canonical branch's tip (that branch stays checked out in the main working tree; `agent.sh branch` accepts the detached HEAD only when it is exactly that tip), with links to the shared batch, approvals, metrics, friction and prompts folders. Night mode creates one per task, runs the session (Claude or the Codex `proofline_night` profile, whose filesystem table now names the worktree's git administration folder) inside it, starts a task only when every dependency is merged, removes the worktree after the merge and keeps a parked task's; a task whose pull request is open and not merged is parked with the reason `awaiting merge`; a second open run in one worktree is still refused (D4) but the message names `worktree-add`; the worktrees are not scratch (A53) and `proofline clean` leaves them alone. (5) *Runtime versions.* `proofline doctor` and the verifier run the read-only `skills/verify-proof/scripts/runtime-versions.sh`, which compares node, dotnet, go and python as installed with what the project's CI specifies (workflow `*-version`, `.nvmrc`, `package.json` engines, `global.json`, `go.mod`, `.tool-versions`, ...); `doctor` prints WARN on a different major (major.minor for go and python), never FAIL; VERIFY.md gets a `## Runtime` section with the script's lines, `validate-verify.mjs` checks the format, and a mismatch never changes the verdict. (6) *The lead writes no product file outside a run.* With no run active the PreToolUse hook denies the main session every write except task files (`tasks.dir`), `.agents/`, the knowledge scope and design documents, git-ignored files and paths outside the project; the denial says to propose a light run with `/proofline run <text>`; the shell scanner judges shell writes (a heuristic) and `proofline doctor` probes both the denial and the task-file pass. (7) *Stop hook scope.* The identifier check (A154) runs only for the final report of a run, the last message of a turn in which the lead ran publish-completion-report, cleanup, terminate, a deliver command or batch-status/batch-check; an ordinary answer is never checked. (8) *One-process approvals.* `agent.sh approve <ID> <KIND>...` takes several kinds in one process (locks and content fingerprint once, each kind recorded as a single `approve` would; a refused kind does not stop the next; none recorded fails), and `approve-pending` makes one call per target with the delivery steps in the order commit, push, pr, merge, cleanup, so the 30 s time limit of a Claude Code UserPromptSubmit hook cannot cut five processes off after the fourth. If a cut-off still leaves a prefix, `deliver-step` stops with a text saying that the reply was recorded only in part, that nothing was run, that the summary is still valid and that the user must send `approve delivery` once more. Why: a red CI used to stop the delivery with a question for a failure the gates could fix; the run's own delivery commit made its plan look stale; one run per worktree blocked every other task behind a parked one and dirtied the main tree; a green local run in another language version proves little; a lead that edits files with no run active defeats the ban on product code (D2); the Stop hook sent the lead back on plain answers; and in a real project the approval hook was cut off before the last step. Rejected: raising the hook time limit (the limit belongs to the runtime and a longer one only moves the cut-off; the fix is less work per call); asking the user at the first red CI (the error is in the log and the gates already bound the fix); an unlimited number of CI-fix rounds (an unbounded loop that pushes without a person); a push approval that covers any ref (a CI fix must not reach another branch); making a runtime mismatch a FAIL (the versions are advice, a different runtime may be intended); one shared working tree with better locking (the open-run, ACTIVE_RUN and hooks state is per worktree); checking every Stop message for identifiers (ordinary answers are not reports). Confidence: medium. Not-tested: a real CI-fix round against a hosted CI (the tests use a fake `gh`), a real Codex session in a task worktree, an approval hook cut off by a real runtime. Amended in round 3: the worktree of a delivered run goes away with the run. `cleanup` (and `deliver-step cleanup`, `deliver-merged`) removes it from inside, once the merge is on record or was proven by the caller and no other run is in it; never for a FAILED or BLOCKED run; `agent.sh cleanup <ID>` in the main working tree removes a worktree an older version or an interrupted cleanup left behind once its merge is in merged.tsv.

- **A170. 0.0.27, design craft: visitor modes, patterns as defaults, a measured design group, source lint and an image ledger (rebalances the 0.0.4 `avoided` rule of A146; amends A81, A82, A158, A166).** What: (1) *Visitor mode.* `ui-design` gives every surface a mode, `persuade`, `operate`, `read` or `experience`, chosen by the surface (a tool's landing page is persuade) and written into the UI spec with a reason; boldness follows the mode, full courage and imagery for persuade and experience, precision and restraint for operate and read. (2) *Idea before design.* Persuade and experience surfaces get a topic inventory of 8-12 things that belong to this product, an argument (one claim and its proof per section, each proof a product fact or a path in the code), and an idea sentence that must stop being true when the nearest rival's name is put into it; three directions dealt by `scripts/deal.mjs` from the bundled library with a recorded seed (the designer derives no candidates, see (9) and (10)) plus the calm category-standard option for the user to choose, and one live interaction with a no-script fallback. (3) *Patterns are defaults.* A dated registry of 15 pattern ids (`Registry date: 2026-10-23`) replaces a ban list: using one needs a line `- <id>: <reason>` under `## Pattern justifications` in `DESIGN.md`; when an ornament goes, fullness, real imagery, motion and craft go in (fullness rule, visual plan, typography, colour, motion thesis, browser surfaces, copy and controls, operate rules, each in a reference file loaded on demand). The 0.0.4 rule `avoided` (A146) is rebalanced, not repealed: `avoided` may still name ids, but absence of ornament is no longer the goal and an empty page is a defect. (4) *Validator.* `validate-ui.mjs` requires the mode, the argument, the inventory, idea, dealt directions (re-dealt from the seed), live thing, visual plan, motion and font plan where the mode demands them, rejects file paths and internal ids as UI copy, headlines over 48 characters and registry misuse; existing fixtures got the new fields, no expected file was loosened. (5) *Design group.* `visual-proof` gets an optional `design` block of `visual.json` and `report.json`, modelled on `seo` (A158): fixed viewports 1440, 768 and 390, checks for heading lines, type scale, body measure, loaded fonts, edge margins, edge text, vacuum, untitled sections, empty hero, theme surfaces, untranslated text, motion count, reduced motion, text without script, pinned scenes photographed at 0, 50 and 100 percent, and the image ledger; a failed item blocks, an item that cannot be measured is `not_measured` with a reason. (6) *Lint and ledger.* `scripts/lint-source.mjs` scans project source for the registry patterns it can detect honestly and writes `lint.json`; a finding is blocking unless `DESIGN.md` justifies its id; `validate-visual.mjs` counts blocking findings as FAIL reasons. `docs/design/IMAGES.md` lists every raster image and self-hosted font with licence and credit or source. (7) *Critique.* COMPLEX and CRITICAL reports with a design group carry 14 judged items, each `ok` or `concern` with a reason and a screenshot; a numeric score is rejected and the critique never closes the gate. (8) *Flow.* The implementer of a UI task runs the auditor, looks at the screenshots with the critique, fixes the three most important problems and repeats at most three rounds (a self-check, never a substitute for QA); for persuade and experience the designer writes `DESIGN.md` first as the direction contract and the knowledge step updates it from the world as built; under `conform` the existing system is unchanged and a redesign needs approval. Why: a site built under 0.0.26 felt like a years-old beginner site (hairline boxes, monospace labels showing file paths, numbered steps, one neon accent on a dark ground, an empty hero, no imagery or motion, untranslated English on a Turkish page); the 0.0.4 `avoided` rule had removed ornaments and put nothing in their place, and nothing measured the result. Rejected: catalogues of looks dressed onto a product (the library below is decisions, picked by a deterministic script, and the idea, rival test and argument steps still force adaptation); an external detector binary (the checks are our own scripts, nothing is installed); a numeric design score (a score invites tuning to the number; the critique is reasoned ok or concern); making image generation mandatory (the visual plan states what is real, and none is allowed). Addendum, same release: (9) *Design library, reversing the 0.0.4/A146 decision of no ready-made style catalogue on purpose.* `skills/ui-design/library/` holds data files from two MIT-licensed sources recorded in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` (the only file that names them, with pinned commits, sha256 per included file and the full licence texts; the static name check excludes exactly that file, the one exception to the third-party-name rule). The included files (directions, heroes, sections, type systems, palettes, motions, app styles, photo sets, the UX guideline list, chart guide, app-interface list and the font-licence directory) are byte-identical copies; our own adaptation layer lives apart in `library/adapt/`, never as edits to the copies; the sources' method documents and their style, palette and colour catalogues are not copied. `tests/ci/sync-design-library.sh` re-fetches at the recorded commits (`--update <source-id> <commit>` moves a pin) and `--check` verifies the copies are byte-identical (tests use a local mirror, no network). Reason for the reversal: the library is not a theme dressed onto a product but composition, typography and motion decisions extracted from real sites, while candidates a model derives from its own habits fall into the same moulds; the idea sentence, the rival test and the argument still force adaptation to the product. (10) *Deal.* `scripts/deal.mjs` replaces designer-derived candidates: inputs are surface mode, sector, tone, the imagery that really exists, section roles and brand constants; it picks three directions with hero, section templates, type system, palette and motion (operate: app style, shell, pattern per screen), never one that needs absent imagery, calls no model and no network, and the same seed gives the same result. A single slot is redrawn only with a written reason (`--redraw <slot> --reason`); content that does not fit a template changes the template, not the content; subject colours replace dealt colours when they clash and the ratios stay. The calm standard option stays beside the three and the designer never recommends it; `ui.json` records inputs, seed, dealt ids and redraws and the validator replays the deal. (11) *Fonts and images.* The library names faces, the implementer self-hosts them and verifies the licence from the font-licence directory or the package's own licence file, writing it to the ledger `## Fonts`; a font whose licence cannot be verified is not used and deal offers a same-voice system that is verifiable. Library photos are used only from sets licensed for commercial use, downloaded and self-hosted, address verified, credit kept on the page and in the ledger; they are never the project's own imagery and never count as deal's existing imagery. (12) *UX rules in QA.* The UX guideline list with its severities becomes a checklist: measurable high-severity rules are measured by the auditor as `design_ux_*` checks, the rest are judged (`ux_review`); `visual-proof` stays installable alone through its own derived `skills/visual-proof/ux-rules.json` (rule id, severity, `measure`, our own short wording) and a test checks every id against the library when both skills are present; the chart guide chooses the chart type for surfaces with charts. (13) *Focus modes.* `/proofline design ui <mode> <target>` with `bolder quieter polish animate typeset colorize layout delight harden adapt` runs like any TRIVIAL or STANDARD task, touches only the target, keeps the system, adds no colour, font or element unless asked, and `scripts/scope-check.mjs` verifies afterwards that nothing outside the target changed. (14) *Comp and model.* When the runtime has an image-generation tool a persuade surface gets a draft visual of the chosen direction before coding, the approved comp is the implementer's target and QA's reference, the skip is written when there is no tool, and generated images enter the ledger; UI tasks with a persuade or experience surface run designer and implementer on the strongest model (signal `ui_persuade`). (15) *Reality check.* Deal was run (seed 7, no model, no network) for three briefs: a restaurant's QR menu site and admin panel fit (three warm photo-led directions with verified fonts; three commerce-style app styles), a developer tool's marketing site and docs fit well (real-UI fragment heroes, quiet and technical directions, none needing photographs), and a city-tour map app was partial: the library has no map-canvas screen pattern, so deal reports none for the map screen and the designer draws it from shell and tokens, while its landing page fits (colour-field and type-poster heroes, no photograph-led template; library photo sets offered self-hosted and credited).
