(16) *Deliberate deviations and hardening.* `design_body_measure` at the phone390 viewport accepts 30-75 characters (a 390 px column cannot hold 45 at a readable size) while 1440 and 768 keep 45-75; a requested design check that ends `not_measured` makes the visual result INCONCLUSIVE (submitted as UNSUPPORTED with a prefixed reason, like core cells), never PASS; every design item's status is validated against its value and threshold, motion_min included; deal flags `photo_dependent` directions (judged from the direction's own text as well as its section tags) and deals one only when nothing else satisfies the brief's imagery, offering the usable library photo sets; the idea sentence must contain the rival's name (`idea.rival`); `scope-check.mjs` uses no rename detection (`--no-renames`), so a rename counts as a delete plus an add; the static name check ignores case, hyphens and spaces and skips only the notices file and the byte-identical copies it lists; library data copies keep the sources' own strings, as the licence requires, which is why those copies are the only other place such text may appear. Rejected, also: hot-linking library photos or fonts (a CDN outage or licence change would break the site; self-hosting is verifiable); copying the sources' method documents (ui-design stays in one voice); taking their style and palette catalogues; a model call inside deal (the pick must be reproducible from the seed). Confidence: medium. Not-tested: real browsers on every viewport in CI (the browser tests skip where none exists), the critique's judgement quality across models, a full persuade-site run end to end.

- **A171. 0.0.28, retro findings of a COMPLEX run (65 scope paths, 7 failed gates, one FAILED run) (amends A76, A148, A157, A159, A169; related A136, A154, A156).** What: 18 findings, in six groups. (A) *Findings and rounds.* (1) A blocking `rules` or `rules+tests` row must carry `scan: <command>` and `instances: single` or the full `path:line` list, or `record` rejects it; `roles/reviewer.md` says so, and script-added rows (evidence starting with `agent.sh`, a prefix `submit` refuses in a reviewer's own rows) are exempt, and a scan must be at least two words and ten characters. A failing record costs no fix round when every blocking row cites a line that already existed in the previously reviewed revision and was not cited before (`gate_carryover_free`, compared by the two fingerprint trees); a re-cited line, a new or changed line (the cited line is mapped through the diff of the two trees and must be unchanged at its position, so a new copy of an old line counts), or a missing earlier tree counts as a round. (2) `GATES.md` has a written "Blocking or info" rule with a version; every gate record stores `blocking_rule`, and `record` rejects an observation that flips between info and blocking while the rule version is unchanged (matched by the cited line's text, or by normalised finding text when the line does not resolve). (3) A mutation budget overrun (21/20) is a `WARNING` line from the validator, printed by `submit`, and no longer blocks. (B) *Gate order and build record.* (4) Gate dependencies are written in `GATES.md` and enforced in `next`, `decide` and `record`: VERIFY needs the QA `visual` focus when the run has one; `pipeline` prints `gate.VERIFY.needs=QA:visual`. (5) `handoff IMPLEMENTED` writes the build record (when build or test is configured; a failing build never blocks the handoff); a missing record is the first step `next` lists. (C) *Knowledge.* (6) Drift in knowledge-scope documents (`DESIGN.md`, `design_docs`) is `info` at the verifier's submit; `knowledge-done` and delivery refuse while design-sync still shows it, when the run has `design/SYNC.md`; no waiver or wider scope is needed. (7) The stale gates after the knowledge step reproduced. Gates, result headers, waivers and `next` now bind `gate_fingerprint`, the content fingerprint without documentation files (`.md`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.yml`, `.txt`) under `knowledge_scope_root` and `design_docs` paths (unless a plan scope names the path; an executable or any other file there stays counted; the documents leave the temporary index in batched calls, so `docs/design/x.sh` binds the gates); approvals, CI and delivery summaries keep the full tree, so the user still approves every byte. A run in flight at upgrade sees its gates stale once. (D) *Approvals and answers.* (8) `approve-pending` writes its output to `.agents/local/approve.log`, shows an unrecorded approval as one line with the reason to the lead and the user, cleans `.approving-` markers older than 2 minutes on the next prompt, and `agent.sh next` records the approval from the user's newest message when the hook could not. (9) Every hook run is timed; the hook spools `name|ms|result` to `.agents/local/hook-times` without a lock and `agent.sh hook-time` moves it into the ledger as one aggregated `hook` event per name plus a `hook-timeout` event per timeout; the friction report counts them. The prompt hook records the capture first, then runs the approval step with a 20 s budget and an 8 s lock wait (`PROOFLINE_HOOK_APPROVE_BUDGET`, `PROOFLINE_HOOK_LOCK_WAIT`; the 20 s default stays because the runtime cuts the hook at 30 s and a normal step takes under a second, so a larger default would only trade a recorded timeout for a killed hook; a step stopped at the budget is never a lost approval, the next `agent.sh next` records it from the captured message, and the self-test pins a 300 s budget so a loaded runner cannot expire it mid-test); a hook the runtime cut off leaves an in-flight marker that the next hook records as a timeout. Measured on a copy of a real project: 0.4 to 0.8 s per prompt hook; the 31 s timeouts came from `approve` waiting up to 120 s for the lock. (10) `answer --captured` takes the newest user message after the question and prints which one (`source_message:` in the answer file). (11) `answer --amend` replaces a recorded answer with a newer, unused user message; the old record is kept as `NNN.answer.amended-K.md` with `amended: true`; stdin is ignored, so the lead alone cannot amend. (12) Run files stay English; the user's own words (answers, approval replies) are stored in a quote block, every line starting with `> `, which the language check exempts in the script-written answer and approval files and in TASK.md, and in any other run file only when the quoted or fenced line repeats a captured user prompt (the 3-letter threshold counts per file in every whole-file scan, at freeze, at submit and at the handoff to DONE; the write-time check sees only the text being written, so a file built from several small edits is caught by those scans, and a per-file edit counter was rejected as state that the scans make redundant); the check runs at write time (`agent.sh language-check` from the write hook for Write, Edit and MultiEdit under `.agents/runs/`), not at delivery. (E) *Size and time.* (13) Freeze stops when the scope has more paths than `pipelines.<CLASS>.max_scope_paths` (TRIVIAL 2, STANDARD 15, COMPLEX 15, CRITICAL 12) and proposes a split; a user answer starting with "proceed without splitting" (no negation or condition), bound to that exact scope list, is recorded as a `split_override` ledger event and lets it continue. (14) The dispatch timeout comes from `dispatch_timeout_seconds` per class (900, 1800, 3600, 3600); the in-flight marker records its own timeout; a timeout writes `dispatch/RESUME-<role>.md` (log tail, changed paths, run artifacts) that the next dispatch of the role carries in its prompt. (F) *Hook and lead.* (15) The hook reads a variable that the same command assigns a plain literal (`ID=T-6; sh agent.sh next $ID`) in argument position, checks the literal like any word (so `c=rec; d=ord; $c$d` is denied as `record`), and allows reading exactly `/tmp/claude-<uid>/<project>/<session>/tasks/<file>.output` as the operand of cat, head, tail, grep, wc or `sed -n '<n>[,<m>]p'` / `sed -n '$p'` (any other sed script is denied; never run, sourced or given to a shell); `printf -v`, `let` and any `IFS` assignment also drop the tracked variables; variables from command substitution, `read`, loops or conditional assignment, a variable as the command word or script path, writes to the task files and `..` stay denied; denials show the allowed form in one line. (16) A bare `agent.sh decide` is refused (`dispatch.sh` writes a nonce file under `.agents/local/dispatch/` holding its own pid for its `decide` call and passes the nonce as `PROOFLINE_DISPATCH`; `agent.sh` accepts it only while the file exists and the pid is alive and an ancestor of the `decide` process, and removes the file on acceptance (one use); a trap removes it if `dispatch.sh` is interrupted and every attempt sweeps nonce files older than a minute; the hook denies any command that names the variable, as written, after removing quotes and variable references, or built from `PROOFLINE` and `DISPATCH` fragments, that names `nonce-` or the nonce folder, or that globs or runs `find` over `.agents` or `.agents/local`); `decide --dry` reads without writing a file or ledger row; `decide --agent-path` records the decision of the Agent route, once per role and focus until a result of exactly that role and focus (the `FOCUS:` header of the raw message) is recorded; the lead's `decide ... --redecide` decides again when the Agent call failed before any result and another runtime or model is wanted (ledger note, the earlier decision file kept, the refusal message shows it); the output starts with `decision: role= runtime= model= effort= reason=`. (17) `agent.sh friction-note <ID> user-command|user-shell` records that the user was asked to run a command, a proofline bug; the friction report counts it and the Stop hook notes such a message when it asks the user to run the command ("please run", "run:", an imperative line, or a fence introduced by one), not when it merely mentions it; a prompt hook stopped at its budget also stops the children of the approval step, by pid. (18) The lead's wait messages are one line (`agent.sh wait-line <ID> [WHAT] [--done]`: `waiting: <what>, <M>m<SS>s so far`). Also fixed: the friction report printed `n/a`, which its own character check rejects, and now says `unknown`; the shared language rule in `tests/shared/shared-rules.md` and every skill carries the quote-block wording. Why: the run's friction report showed VERIFY failing 3 times and REVIEW_RULES 4 times, 7 gate failures, 4 asks, 3 fix rounds and a dispatch timeout; the lead and the user did work that scripts can do. The evidence folder of the run was cleaned before the fix, so each item is shown from the code and the friction report. Rejected: matching the "same class" of a finding by its text (too fuzzy to be deterministic); making the whole next failing record free (an unfixed line could loop); re-binding gate records after the knowledge step (it weakens the record; excluding the files is simpler, with approvals still bound to the whole tree); expanding variables used as command words (an obfuscation vector); trusting any variable; a hook-only decide check (the script is the foundation); a second quote syntax; a CLI flag for the split override (not user-backed); a per-call ledger line for hook timings; telling the user to run `approve` in a terminal; keeping "oldest unused message" for `--captured`; editing the old answer file; blocking the Stop hook (A154 chose no rewrite loop). Confidence: medium. Not-tested: a real runtime kill of the prompt hook (simulated with a dead in-flight marker), the full self-test under load (CI runs it).
- **A172. 0.0.29, one identity for ids and a language check that lets Turkish (or any) product text be quoted (amends A33, A171; related A107, A129, A130).** What: (A) *Ids.* `agent.sh submit` gave a QA plan step (a task result, `kind=task`) the finding prefix `QA-` because it took the gate prefix from `gate_of` for every role, while `record` demanded `qa-` (`^<role>-<n>$`, case-sensitive) for a task result, so every QA plan step with findings was rejected after its report was written; reproduced with `AS qa submit LC --result DONE --findings <rows>`: `invalid finding id QA-1 (want qa-<n>)`. Now `result_kind ROLE RESULT` (gate or task, one rule) and `finding_prefix ROLE KIND GATE` (`<GATE>` for a gate result, `<role>` for a task result) are the only places that decide, and both `submit` (writes) and `record` (demands) call them; the gate ids (`QA-1`, `REVIEW_TESTS-2`, `SECURITY-1`) and the task ids (`explorer-3`, `qa-1`) do not change (`roles/README.md`). Ids are compared by key through `id_key`, `id_eq` and `id_keys` in `agent.sh` and `idKey` in each node validator (skills share no files): upper case, leading zeros of the number dropped (`AC-01` is `ac-1`); the form the producer wrote is canonical, is recorded as written and is accepted as written. Same-kind mismatches found and fixed: the `record` prefix and duplicate checks (case); `waive`, `request-approval waive:<id>` and `approve waive:<id>` (an id typed in another case matched nothing although the approval words are lower-cased; now matched by key and used as recorded, `waive_canon` and `canon_kind`); the completion report checks `report_names_id` and `report_key_lines` (a line `qa-1` or `review_rules` did not name `QA-1` or `REVIEW_RULES`); `verify_qa_plan_bound`, `qa_invalid_missing`, `plan_test_acs` and the assumption duplicate check in `agent.sh`; `validate-qa.mjs` (scenario, criterion and report ids), `validate-plan.mjs` (criteria, `## Tests`, `visual_proof`, assumption ids), `validate-tdd.mjs` (cycle criteria against scope criteria), `validate-verify.mjs` (AC coverage rows against TASK, PLAN scope and `visual_proof`), test-trust (`validate-findings.mjs` and `gate.mjs`: criteria against claim mutants), evidence-map (assumption ids), ui-design (`validate-ui.mjs`: criteria against the task), visual-proof (`validate-visual.mjs`: PLAN `visual_proof` against criteria), product-spec (`check-prd.mjs` exports `idKey`; `check-coverage.mjs` and `trace.mjs`: `Covers:` against FR and NFR ids, `trace fr-1`), task-author (`Covers:` ids) and the three `validate-product-claims.mjs` copies (`ref slug#c-1` was accepted by the regex and then searched case-sensitively in the claims file). Also: a `qa` BLOCKED result takes the task prefix in `submit` as in `record` but still reports in `QA_REPORT.md`. (B) *Language.* The check (A171) exempted a quote or fence line only when it repeated a captured user message, so a Turkish site's acceptance criteria, QA plan and review findings, which must quote the site text, made agents transliterate it to ASCII or ask the user. Now inline code, a double-quoted span (`"..."` or curly quotes), a `> ` line, a fenced line and a JSON string value are exempt when their whole inner text, whitespace normalized, occurs in the run's `TASK.md`, the captured user messages or a product file COMMITTED to git outside `.agents/` (`git grep -I` on `HEAD`, never the index, the working tree or an untracked file; capped at 50 MB), and is at least 4 characters and matches on word boundaries (no letter right before or after the piece). The match is on the inner text as one piece, so a model cannot hide a sentence of its own behind a delimiter. The minimum is 4 characters: a piece of 1 to 3 characters occurs in almost any file and proves nothing, its letters still count towards the three-letter limit, and 4 keeps real labels such as a button text quotable. Performance: a file is first scanned without the product text (one awk pass, an English write costs what it cost before); only a file with a hit looks its quoted pieces up, and no piece is searched on its own: a piece with a word that no corpus holds is dropped by a sorted word-list comparison, the few left are searched in one pass with one alternation pattern, and the committed text (marked at word boundaries, with its word list) is cached per HEAD commit in `.agents/local/language/`; 300 non-matching spans over an 8 MB corpus take about 0.1 s warm and 1.7 s on the first call of a commit. A piece longer than 1000 characters is never exempt. The cache is a file, and a runtime with no write hook (Codex) can edit it, so it only pre-filters: each piece it accepts is confirmed with one `git grep -I -E` on `HEAD` (word boundaries kept, whitespace runs match any whitespace run, deduplicated pieces, no line scanning); a forged hit is refused by the confirmation and a forged miss only refuses a quote. Consequence, stated plainly: text a task writes into new or changed files cannot be quoted until it is committed, except through `TASK.md`; put it in `TASK.md` to quote it, and a quote must lie within one line of a committed file. The machine-output exemption is an accepted, unchecked channel: a role allowed to write under `reviews/visual-proof/` or `reports/qa-evidence/` could put text there. The write hook passes the target path so the run of a stdin write is known. Machine output of the tools is exempt (`reviews/visual-proof/` and `reports/qa-evidence/`, checked against `roles/qa.md` `owns:` and the visual-proof skill), like dispatch output, scratch, gates and the ledger already were. Every role's must-not row, the shared language rule of all 28 skills and the `AGENTS.md` block now say: never translate or transliterate product text or a quote to ASCII, and never ask the user about it; `language_fail_text` shows the quote path instead of a translation. visual-proof reports Turkish typed without its letters (`degil`, `icin`, `Turkce`, ...) on a `design.languages` page whose `lang` is Turkish as `design.language_notes` and one `info` row, never blocking and not a design check (so the expected-check sets do not change); the list and an allow list are the new `visual.ascii_turkish_words` and `visual.ascii_turkish_allow` of `.agents/config.yaml` (`cfg`, i.e. `agent.sh config-get`, reads them, `config-check` validates them, `measure.mjs` reads the same file, else the built-in list). Why: the first made every QA plan step with a finding fail after the work was done; the second made agents damage the text they had to quote or ask the user a question with no real choice. Rejected: forcing every id to lower case (it renames the gate ids `QA-1` and `REVIEW_RULES-2` that the ledger, waivers and reports already carry); recording the checker's form instead of the producer's (two spellings of one finding); opening the quote exemption completely (a model could write its own non-English text behind a backtick, a quote or a fence, the A171 review finding); matching a piece by a word list or language detection (not deterministic); including untracked files (`git grep --untracked`) or the index or working tree (`git ls-files`, `git grep` without a tree): an agent can write its own non-English text into a file and quote it, and `git add` makes it tracked and staged without a commit; only committed content counts (a file created in the same run counts once it is committed, which a model cannot do); the user's messages as the only corpus (the site text is rarely in them); a new design check for ASCII-ized words (it would change the expected items of every report for an information-only finding); a per-line corpus read and `grep -F -f` over the corpus (measured: 33 s for 300 patterns on 12 MB with the grep of the development machine; its speed is not portable). Also fixed in review: `validate-qa.mjs` matched a failure id by substring (`QA-1` was satisfied by `QA-10`); it now matches the exact id by key. Confidence: medium. Not-tested: the time of `git grep` on a very large repository (capped at 50 MB, and only when a file already has a hit); the Codex runtime (its hook set has no write-time language check).

- **A173. 0.0.30, proofline never assumes or imposes a project folder layout: one ecosystem definition, pruned discovery, no broken command (related A147, A172; amends the 0.0.26 runtime versions and D8 discovery; continued in A174 to A177).** What: (1) *One definition.* `control-plane/agents/ecosystems.json` (installed as `.agents/ecosystems.json`) describes ten ecosystems (JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Go, Java/Kotlin, Rust, .NET, PHP, Ruby, Swift, Dart/Flutter): prune dirs, project files, manifests, locks, package-source settings, workspace roots, solution files, version files, risky paths, command templates, benchmark and native-UI markers and test-output patterns. Adding an ecosystem is one object. sh scripts read `ecosystems.tsv`, its flat form generated by `node ecosystems.mjs write` (`scripts/ecosystems.sh`: `eco_get`, `eco_children`, `eco_pack`, `eco_rows`, ...), node scripts read the JSON (`ecosystems.mjs`). Skills are installable alone, so a skill carries byte-identical copies, and `tests/shared/check-shared.sh` compares them and checks the flat file against the JSON. (2) *Discovery.* `bin/lib/discover.sh` searches without a depth limit but does not enter build output, dependency and tool folders; it recognises workspace roots (a workspace stands for its members); the root is the target and is run bare, otherwise exactly one outermost nested project is the target and the command is fully targeted (`npm --prefix web test`, `go -C svc test ./...`, `cargo test --manifest-path core/Cargo.toml`); this is decided per ecosystem, and zero or several targets of an ecosystem produce no candidate for it (`init` names it; the 0.0.5 flow asks the user once). .NET targets files: root solutions, root projects, nested solutions, nested projects, `.slnx` before a same-name `.sln`, `*.csproj`, `*.fsproj` and `*.vbproj`, `dotnet format <target> --verify-no-changes` when a root `.editorconfig` exists, and the CI lint pattern catches `dotnet format ... --verify-no-changes`. A path with a space or unusual character is never a candidate. A `justfile` and a `Taskfile` are read like the `Makefile`. Each ecosystem adds its own command, so a root .NET solution and a nested npm app give a list (A176); a root project no longer hides a nested project of another ecosystem. (3) *Runtime versions.* `runtime-versions.sh` reads the definition: the version files and presence markers of every ecosystem are found at the root and nested (pruned, 6 levels, 400 files); a project only under `obj/` or `bin/` is ignored; java, rust, php, ruby, swift and dart join node, dotnet, go and python (`validate-verify.mjs` accepts any lower-case runtime name). Why: .NET 10 creates `.slnx`; the maxdepth-2 search missed `src/Api/Api.csproj` and proposed a bare `dotnet build` that fails with MSB1011 or MSB1003; and the same assumption (a root layout) was in every other ecosystem's checks. Rejected: a depth limit (hides real layouts); guessing the first of several candidates (a broken command in the gate); a JSON parser in sh or node as a requirement of `init` (init works without node); one big shared file read by skills at `../../` (a skill must work installed alone); hard-coding the ecosystems again in each script (the drift this removes). Known limits: only one target per ecosystem is proposed (a second project of the same ecosystem gets none); the definition's `risky_paths`, `manifests`, `benchmark` and `native_ui` sections are consumed by A174 and `test_output` by A175; a Ruby project below the root and a nested Dart or Flutter test have no targeted form, so they give no candidate; `dotnet test` in Microsoft.Testing.Platform mode may need `--solution`/`--project` (and on .NET 10 the project needs `global.json` `test.runner`, A175) and is dropped by `--verify-commands` when it fails; discovery costs about 0.45 s per project because it is plain sh.
- **A174. 0.0.30, risky paths, dependency manifests, benchmark and native-UI markers come from the ecosystem definition (related A78, A88, A162, A173).** What: `review.risky_paths` and the `dependencies` risk signal take the ecosystem globs (manifests, locks, package-source settings, build-changing files) from `.agents/ecosystems.tsv` at read time; `config.yaml` keeps only project-specific globs and the kinds the definition lacks (mix, conan, vcpkg, deno, CMake). One synthetic line, `risk.ecosystems.dependencies`, binds the set into `freeze.risk_sha256`; a run frozen before keeps its paths and passes `verify-freeze` (four accepted hash forms, the A162 precedent). `diff-manifests.mjs` (exploit-proof) classifies a file by the definition, reads every manifest kind of the ten ecosystems and the package-source settings as `index:<host>` entries, and a project `.agents/ecosystems.json` beats the skill copy. design-sync, `probe_performance` (no `head -50`, no depth or count limit) and visual-proof native detection (MAUI only when `UseMaui` is true) read the same list. Why: the lists lived in config, in `diff-manifests.mjs` and in each probe, so `*.fsproj`, `Directory.Build.props`, a Gradle version catalog or the 55th project of a solution were invisible to one of them. Rejected: a second glob list in `config.yaml` (it drifts); rewriting user configs on upgrade (the config cannot be merged below two levels, and the read-time union needs no edit). Known limits: no doctor warning for a missing `ecosystems.tsv` (the lists then fall back to the config values and a benchmark or native probe reports nothing); MAUI is measured only through the project's own Maestro flows.
- **A175. 0.0.30, test-output classes come from the ecosystem definition and real runner output (related A147, A173).** What: `classify-red.mjs` reads the `test_output` section of `ecosystems.json` through the skill-local copy instead of a pattern list in the script. Every entry names its runner and its evidence: `source: captured` (a fixture in `tests/skills/fixtures/tdd-proof-output` with tool, version, command and exit code in its header) or `source: docs` (the tool's own documentation or source, the tool was not installed). No guess is kept; what neither backs is listed under "Not covered" in `skills/tdd-proof/references/RED.md`. An entry may carry `unless`, a pattern that cancels it when the output also shows a test ran, so one package's `[no test files]` or one cargo target's `running 0 tests` cannot hide another's failing assertion. `--exit-code` and `--ecosystem` are cross-checks only: exit 0 never leaves an assertion RED, and a code listed for exactly one of `no_tests` and `compile` names that class (pytest and unittest 5, Microsoft.Testing.Platform 8, dart test 79); an exit code never yields `assertion`. Facts found on .NET 10: VSTest exits 0 when nothing ran, also when `--filter` matches nothing; Microsoft.Testing.Platform exits 8; an MTP project without `global.json` `"test": {"runner": ...}` fails to build and is `compile`. Also: `proofline doctor` no longer reads `runtime: none` as a runtime, and the doctor fresh-install test got a fixture without a runtime (`sc_doctor_fresh` is split into a Node and a no-runtime fixture); it was wrong on main too, because `base_build` writes a `package.json`. Why: the patterns were a seed nobody had checked against real output; with the 94 recorded runs, 36 were classified wrong or `unknown` before the change (zero tests under VSTest exits 0, a filter that matched nothing, a second package hiding a failing assertion). Rejected: keeping a guessed pattern or exit code (a false RED is a proof that proves nothing; it is listed as not covered instead); exit code as evidence of RED. Known limits: captured runners are node:test, bun, vitest, tsc, unittest, go test, Minitest, test-unit, swift test and the .NET SDK 10.0.402 with xunit.v3, xunit 2, NUnit and MSTest in both modes; jest, mocha, pytest, Maven, Gradle, JUnit, cargo, PHPUnit, RSpec and dart/flutter test come from documentation; the unverified items are in RED.md and in the [ecosystem matrix](concepts/ecosystems.md#ecosystem-matrix).
- **A176. 0.0.30, several commands per key: `commands.build|test|lint` accept a list (related A148, A173).** What: each of the three keys takes one command (a scalar, unchanged) or a block list of `- command` lines, for a project with more than one stack (a .NET backend and a React frontend). One reader, `cfg_cmds` (`config-get` prints the items one per line), serves `agent.sh` and `bin/lib/config.sh`; `config-check` validates the shape and rejects a value plus a list, an empty item, a duplicate, an inline `[a, b]` and a list under `install` or `secret_scan`. `build-record` and the verify re-run run every command of a key even when an earlier one fails, report each (`build[2/3]`, its exit, its output tail and a `failed:` line), and a failed key still stops the next key. Discovery adds one command per ecosystem (a root .NET solution plus a nested npm app give a list); an ambiguous ecosystem gets none and `init` names it; a Makefile, justfile, Taskfile, CI or README command covers the whole repository and is then the only candidate for its kind; a root project no longer beats a nested project of another ecosystem. `init --verify-commands` drops a failing item, not the list. Why: the single string forced a polyglot repository to pick one stack, and the other stack was never built or tested by the gate. Rejected: an inline `[a, b]` (a command may start with a bracket); reads of the first item only by consumers that do not know the list (a silent gap in the gate).
- **A177. 0.0.30, a suite cannot go red from a dying scenario: `run_sc` propagates failure (related A173).** What: `run_sc` in `tests/cli/cli-test.sh` ran a scenario as `( "$@"; printf ... )`, so a scenario that died exited 0 and the whole cli suite could never fail in `selftest.sh`; it now remembers a failed scenario, runs the others and exits non-zero at the end, and a scenario of its own tests that. Why: `sc_doctor_fresh` looked broken on main only when run directly, and nothing in the suite had ever shown it.
- **A178. 0.0.30, the question block the script stores for the user is exempt from the language scan (amends A171, A172; related A99, A103).** What: `agent.sh ask` and `record` (a specialist's NEEDS_INPUT) write the question block to `questions/NNN.md`; in a Turkish run (A99) the script itself prints it in the user's language, and `verify_run_language` then refused `handoff DONE` because of it, while the lead cannot edit run files. `language_scan` now skips exactly `.agents/runs/<ID>/questions/NNN.md` (the remainder after the run folder is compared whole, so `results/questions/001.md` or `reviews/a/questions/001.md` is not exempt, and no other file of `questions/` is), and the write-time hook compares the same way; the front-matter lines (`from`, `focus`, `grill`, `result`, `asked_at`) stay English because the script writes them. Every other script-written run file was checked: `approvals/` and requests hold ids, hashes and times only, `waivers/` hold the lead's English `--reason`, `decisions/`, `dispatch/` and `ledger` are machine output and already exempt, `deliver/` and friction notes live under `.agents/local/`, which the scan does not read; the `.answer.md` files are quote blocks (A171). Why: a file addressed to the user in the user's language by design cannot also be English. Residual: the text of a question is not checked. A specialist's NEEDS_INPUT block reaches that file through `record`, so a specialist could put non-English text into its question; it is shown only to the user, is never evidence and is read by no gate. No role can write the file itself (the hook denies `questions/*` to every writer but `agent.sh`), so the hook line is a consistency guard, not a reachable path. Rejected: translating the stored question (the user is shown the stored text verbatim); exempting all of `questions/` (a note dropped there would escape the check).
- **A180. 0.0.32, platform-independent delivery: GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, and a hand-off everywhere else (amends A136, A163).** What: `platform.sh` reads the origin URL (GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, Bitbucket, other) from exact hosts only, so `github.com.evil.example` is `other`; `PROOFLINE_PLATFORM=github|gitlab|azure|bitbucket|other` names a self-hosted host. With the matching tool on PATH (gh, glab, az) proofline opens the pull or merge request and `proofline merge` applies the same fail-closed rule: open, not a draft, every check green on the head being merged, the head read twice. gh merges with `--match-head-commit` and glab with `--sha`; az has no such option. Without the tool, or on Bitbucket and other hosts, nothing is merged: the branch is pushed, the link and the steps are printed, the user merges, and the delivery has only commit, push and pr. A pull request with no checks (no rollup, pipeline or build policy) is merged only after `commands.build` and `commands.test` pass in a clean export of the exact commit (`build-record.sh run <sha>`); the description, the delivery summary (`ci: verified locally, no CI`) and a note on the request say so. "No CI" in batch, doctor, the summary and next-user is a warning; the `ci` next-step state and the batch BLOCKER are removed. The runtime hook denies `glab mr merge`, glab api merge endpoints and `glab alias`, `az repos pr` with `--auto-complete`, `--bypass-policy` or `--status completed`, `az rest` and `az devops invoke` aimed at pull requests, and HTTP clients (curl, wget, http, xh, aria2c) aimed at a merge-request or pull-request merge or completion path. The HTTP rule is method-blind by design: it matches the endpoint shape and ignores the verb, because the verb is easy to hide and a read of those endpoints is never needed. Why: users on GitLab, Azure, Bitbucket or without CI could not use delivery at all, and the single merge path must stay single. Rejected: a `--no-ci` or `--admin` override (overrides the evidence instead of replacing it); skipping the merge check when there is no CI (green would be unproven); a Bitbucket adapter (no first-party CLI); files alone as the CI truth for the merge decision (the platform is the truth, files only hint at the warning); CI-fix rounds on GitLab and Azure (the failed-log reader is gh-only, so it stops with a message). Residuals: az has no match-head option, so a push between the second read and the completion is not refused by az (the head is read twice only); glab's own auto-merge flag was not verified (glab was not installed), which is safe because the call is reached only with a final success pipeline or none, so there is nothing to wait for; Azure CI presence is `unknown` from files. Amended in round 3: a local origin (an absolute or relative path, or a `file://` URL, for example a bare repository on disk) is a valid origin on platform `other` (`platform.sh field local`); it used to stop `deliver-plan` with "not a hosting service address". The delivery has the steps commit, push, pr; the pr step is a hand-off ("merge the branch into origin's canonical branch, for example `git push origin <branch>:<base>`"), proofline merges nothing, and with no CI the local verification of this decision stays (`build-record.sh run <sha>`). A host-shaped origin that is not readable is still refused, and a configured `cli` platform is never applied to a local origin. Amended in round 4: the origin url comes from one helper (`origin_url` in agent.sh) that resolves a relative local path (`../origin.git`) against the MAIN working tree, because git resolves it against the working directory and the shared config means another folder in a run worktree; `deliver-merged` fetches that absolute url, and the push command shown for a relative origin is `git push <absolute-url> <branch>[:<base>]` (a direct url: `-c remote.origin.url` adds a second url, so git also pushed to the relative one and failed from a worktree; the shared config is not rewritten; the pre-push hook works on refs, and the runtime push guard reads the first word as the repository, so both still apply). Documentation-only tasks (verdict, no code change): supported by design when the pages are in the plan scope (`new: true`); the knowledge step cannot prove an acceptance criterion because it runs after the gates (docs/concepts/workflow.md). Amended in round 5: for a relative local origin the approved `deliver-step push` runs the push itself (exactly this delivery's branch to its own ref, to the absolute url; the canonical branch is refused; the step consumes the push approval first and skips the pre-push hook for that one command), because the runtime push guard refuses a push to an absolute path outside the project when the model types it. Correction in round 5: the rebuilt hand-off takes the delivered branch's CURRENT head (never the summary's head, which is HEAD before the commit step and already on origin's canonical branch); a branch that cannot be found or has no commit beyond the summary's head records nothing. Round 6: the squash/rebase proof also needs a commit on origin's tip touching the delivered paths after the run's base, an empty delivery (head equals the base) is never recorded, the relative-origin push sends the approved head commit (`<head>:refs/heads/<branch>`, with `--`), the summary pins `origin_url` and the push refuses when it changed, an origin url starting with `-` is refused, and local-origin detection needs `/`, `./`, `../` or `file:///` (a bare name resolves against the main tree like `origin_url`).
- **A181. 0.0.32, night mode runs in the same session; the headless driver is removed (amends A157, A163).** What: `/proofline batch <ID...|all>` no longer starts a detached driver. After the one "approve batch" (same summary, hash binding and coverage; CRITICAL excluded) the lead runs each task and delivers it in dependency order, and the next task starts only when the previous one is merged (`merged.tsv`). A stuck task is parked (open question, FAILED or BLOCKED, uncovered approval, open PR, or `batch-park`), its dependents are skipped, independent ones go on. New: read-only `agent.sh batch-next [--tsv]` derives the state from records only (merged.tsv, runs, questions, approvals, ci.tsv, state.tsv) and ends with `NEXT: run|resume|cover|deliver|ci|finished|approve|wait`; the lead calls it before every task, so it survives a compaction. The same digest is what the lead re-reads; also `batch-ci <ID>` (one-shot CI check of the merge commit), `batch-awake` and `batch-park`, `batch-plan --replace`. Review round 1 added: the merged record is written before the run cleanup; one session per batch (an `owner` file; only the lead claims or is told to wait, any other role gets the digest and writes nothing; a dead owner is taken over; no findable session process means no guard); a merge whose record is missing is recovered from the platform with `agent.sh pr-state`. `batch-awake` runs `caffeinate -i -w <session pid>` on macOS (systemd-inhibit on Linux) so the machine stays awake exactly as long as the session. Interruption (session closed, limit, sleep) just stops; `/proofline batch` continues the approved batch and never re-runs a merged task. Why: a driver needed process groups, a sandbox profile, timeouts and a runtime fallback, while the lead session already has the user's permissions and context, and the user can watch it. Removed: `batch.sh run|start|stop` and the `_driver`, `_session` and `_pgprobe` helpers, the LOCK, driver.pid, stop.req and driver logs, the sandbox profile `proofline_night`, `--codex-danger-full-access`, runtime fallback with usage-limit and auth detection, the `agent.sh batch-start` and `batch-stop` commands (`proofline batch run|stop` print what to do), the driver states in next-user, and the driver tests. `batch.task_timeout` and `batch.runtimes` are still accepted by `config-check` and ignored, so existing configs stay valid (not validated). Rejected: keeping the driver as an option (two code paths and the sandbox surface stay); a state.tsv written by the lead at every change (derived from records instead, so a forgotten write cannot desync); a blocking CI wait inside one command (tool call limit, the lead loops). Not verified: a `caffeinate` started from the agent's shell tool surviving the call and finding the `claude` or `codex` ancestor (tests use `PROOFLINE_SESSION_PID`). Amended in round 3: a manual merge is recorded from git. The pr step of a delivery where the user merges keeps the delivered commit in `deliver/<ID>/MERGE_HEAD`; `agent.sh deliver-merged <ID>` (and `--check`, which batch-next uses) fetches origin's canonical branch and proves the merge: the delivered commit is an ancestor of `origin/<base>`, or every path the delivery changed has identical content at origin's tip (squash or rebase merge); anything else is "not merged" (a batch parks the task as `awaiting merge` and says what to run). Proven, it writes `merged.tsv` (PR field `-`), fast-forwards the local canonical branch when the main working tree sits on it, clean, and cleans the run up, so `batch-next` moves on (`NEXT: deliver <ID> merged` between the user's merge and that record). Amended in round 5: `deliver-merged` rebuilds a missing `MERGE_HEAD` hand-off from the delivery summary (branch, base and head the user approved; it is missing when the pr step did not run, for example when the user pushed and merged by hand), and always fetches origin's canonical branch itself through the absolute url helper, so `/proofline batch` continues without any manual git command. Round 6: the worktree of a run is removed only when this run's merge is on record (a merged.tsv row of the ID not older than the delivery summary; an environment variable never counts), without `--force`, and not when it holds untracked or ignored files other than the known copies of worktree-prep.
- **A182. 0.0.32, per-surface design documents: `design_docs.design` can be a mapping (related A170).** What: `design_docs.design` stays a path, or becomes a mapping with an optional `shared` base and `surfaces.<name>.doc|paths|mode`. One resolver decides the surface of a file: `agent.sh design-surface <PATH>` (read-only `key=value` lines); `design-sync.mjs --file` follows the same rules and is tested against the same cases. Overlap between surfaces exits 1; no match means the shared document only, with a warning when there is no shared one; a matched surface with no document is `new-direction`, designed on the shared base and never conformed to another surface. Glob rule: `*` and `**` match any characters including `/`, and `**/` also matches zero directories; a `paths` glob may contain only one `**/` (`config-check` rejects `apps/**/x/**/y`), and no `\`, `|`, absolute or `..` path. The shared and every surface document are `design_docs` paths, so knowledge scope, the runtime hook and the content fingerprint read them through `design_doc_paths`. `ui-design` proposes two modes with one question when a surface mixes visitor modes. Why: one product often has surfaces with different visitor modes (persuade and operate), and one DESIGN.md forces one of them to conform to the other. Rejected: a list of maps (`config_lines` cannot parse it; named maps flatten to dotted keys with no parser change); glob logic in each consumer (drift between shell and JS); a new top-level key (breaks existing configs and default roots); a hook-only allow-list for surface documents (enforcement lives in `agent.sh`).
- **A183. 0.0.32, Codex support labels follow recorded evidence (amends A140).** What: the labels "experimental" and "partially tested" for Codex are replaced by what a real project recorded (2026-10-23 to 2026-10-25, `.agents/local/metrics`, `proofline_version` 0.0.28 in that project's config): 26 dispatch records, 17 of Codex as implementer (13 submitted, 2 failed, 2 timed out) and 9 of Claude as implementer (8 submitted, 1 timed out). Codex is in 13 step records, all in the implementer role (9 done, 4 blocked); the other 140 step records and every lead record are Claude. TASK-007 to TASK-010 had Codex implementer work that passed the gates and was merged (TASK-008 and TASK-009 entirely by Codex dispatches); TASK-006 timed out on Codex and Claude finished it. Failover from Codex to Claude happened in use (TASK-006, TASK-007, TASK-010; the friction report counts 2 runtime failovers). The new labels: Codex as implementer is supported; Codex as lead, reviewer, qa, architect, designer, explorer, verifier and security reviewer is "not yet verified in real use"; failover works in real use for Codex to Claude, while Claude to Codex stays covered only by the dispatch test. Nothing else is claimed. The records do not name the cause of the failures (a usage limit is not recorded), so none is stated. Why: a label should say what was observed and the old rows (a scored Codex-only TRIVIAL failure, then runs ended by a usage limit) predate this use. Rejected: calling all Codex configurations supported (only the implementer role was seen); keeping "experimental" (it hides real merged work). The dated e2e rows stay as history.
- **A184. 0.0.33, path classification follows the git worktree root; an explorer's report is a claims table (amends A169).** What: (1) a path inside a run's own worktree (`<main>/.agents/local/worktrees/<ID>/...`) is judged relative to THAT worktree's root, so the lead may write `EVIDENCE.md` and the other lead artifacts under the worktree's `.agents/runs/<ID>/`, `RUN.yaml`, gates, approvals, questions, dispatch records stay protected exactly as in the main tree, and the worktree's own `.agents/local/**` stays runtime state (denied). The one definition is `agent.sh worktree-root <ABS-PATH>` (read-only, every role): it answers only for a folder that is exactly `<main working tree>/.agents/local/worktrees/<ID>`, is registered by `git worktree list` of this project, is a linked worktree of the same common git-dir, is not a link, and contains the physical path; otherwise exit 1. The runtime hook's `relpath` (the single place every hook check, shell write scan and Write/Edit check resolves a path through) calls it for paths under `.agents/local/worktrees/*/*` and keeps the old project-relative path (denied as runtime state) on any doubt: agent.sh missing, folder not registered, crafted folder, nested worktree. The hook resolves symlinks first, so the shared links (`batch approvals metrics friction prompts`) land in the main tree's `.agents/local/**` and stay denied. Every classification inside agent.sh, the pre-commit hook and the content fingerprint works on paths that git reports relative to the working tree it runs in (the run's own worktree), so they were already correct and need no helper; the other `.agents/...` mentions in `bin/`, `batch.sh`, `dispatch.sh` and `next-user.sh` build explicit locations and classify nothing. (2) An explorer's DONE report is the claims table of evidence-map (`| id | severity | path:line | finding | evidence |`), with a concrete example in the role and in the dispatch assignment; when a report is prose, `agent.sh submit` still records it and prints a NOTE, and the lead sends the same explorer back (or re-dispatches the same assignment) to redo it as the table and never writes `EVIDENCE.md` from prose. Why: the first real same-session batch denied the lead's `EVIDENCE.md` write because the main-root path began with `.agents/local`; and a lead that rewrote prose reports itself produced claims nobody verified. Rejected: allowing `.agents/local/worktrees/**` by string match (a crafted folder would open `.agents/local`); a copy of the logic in the hook (it would drift; the hook asks agent.sh instead); refusing prose at `submit` (existing explorers and answer-only tasks submit prose; a NOTE keeps them working while the lead rule closes the gap). Known limit: while a run is active in the main tree, the in-run rule compares against that run id only, so the lead's write to another task's worktree run is judged like a write to another run in the main tree. Amended in review: when the session's project root is itself a run worktree (the runtime sets it so), a path inside the MAIN working tree of the same git common dir that is not inside the session's own worktree is judged with the main tree's rules, relative to the main tree (`.agents/local/**`, run approvals and gates stay protected), never as "outside the project" (which let the lead write the main tree's `.agents/local/approvals`); in the main tree nothing changes. Amended in round 2: from CODE_DONE on, `task_changed_paths` leaves out a knowledge-scope file (docs/wiki, design documents, ADR) that the plan does not name, so the knowledge step's output never raises the tier, the risk signals or the gates (a small run whose wiki pages pushed it to full could neither record the four new gates nor leave CODE_DONE: `amend` needs every gate to pass); before CODE_DONE such a file still counts and `verify-scope` reports it. If a gate of the effective tier is still unsatisfied for the task-owned patch at CODE_DONE, `agent.sh next` says so (only `amend` with passing gates, or a new task; no reviewer dispatch) instead of offering the knowledge step, and the `not_applicable` refusal names the cheap path (a one-page note under docs/wiki/ changes no tier). Round 6: after CODE_DONE only a regular, non-executable, non-symlink file with a documentation extension (md mdx rst adoc html txt, images) that the plan does not name is knowledge output; any other file under the knowledge scope (a script, a link) still counts for tier, risk and gates.
- **A185. 0.0.33, one run state per worktree, shared state by path, dependency and env preparation (amends A169, A184).** What: (1) *One source per kind of state.* The state of one run (`.agents/runs`, `ACTIVE_RUN`, deliver, assignments, locks and, for the runtime hook, windows, records, submissions, baseline, hook-times, in-flight marks) lives in the worktree that owns the run. The hook computes `sroot`: the root of the run worktree that contains the path the tool touches (Write, Edit and the like) when that path is inside the project, else the one that contains the event's working directory, as answered by `agent.sh worktree-root` (A184); anything else is the project root, where nothing changes. It then asks that worktree's `agent.sh`, so `window-open`, `window-close`, `hook-time`, `summary`, `next` and the approval step work on the run folder the session itself uses. A command from the main tree that names a run in a worktree was already forwarded there (A169). Run paths the hook reads (`PLAN.md` scope, `owns.conf`, run approvals, untracked-file baseline) follow `sroot`. A lead writing from the main tree into a worktree's run is now judged against that worktree's run (this removes the "known limit" of A184). A Bash command's directory change inside one call is not seen: the working directory of the event decides. State that belongs to no run (`batch approvals metrics friction prompts`, and the `-` approvals) lives only in the main working tree; `agent.sh` reaches it through `shared_dir` and the scripts through `PROOFLINE_SHARED_ROOT`, the hook through `shared_local`, all by path. The worktree no longer gets links to those folders; the shared lock of the main tree is taken as well as the worktree's, so concurrent writers from two trees serialise. In the main tree `sr_main` is the root: byte-identical there. (2) *Dependencies.* `ecosystems.json` gets one new per-ecosystem key, `worktree_deps.folders` (plain relative folder names; `node_modules` for npm, `vendor` for php, `vendor/bundle` for ruby, empty where the folder is not relocatable or a cache lives outside the project), validated by `ecosystems.mjs`. `worktree-prep.sh` (called by `worktree-add`, also on reuse) copies each listed folder that the main tree has, git ignores and does not track; a link left by an earlier version is replaced by the copy; an absolute link inside the copy that points into the main tree is re-pointed at the worktree. A task that changes dependencies never alters the main tree's. (3) *Local files.* `worktree.copy_files` (default `.env*`, `none` = off, validated by `config-check`) names untracked files copied into the worktree; only a file that git ignores in both trees is copied, the rest is reported. `.agents/local/worktree-copied` lists them and the pre-commit hook refuses any staged path in it (humans too). Evidence is written from tracked and changed paths, which exclude ignored files; the secret scan is not changed and still sees such a file whenever it is among the changed paths. (4) *Windows.* No sharing depends on a symlink any more: where `ln -s` fails or silently copies (Git Bash without developer mode), state is read from the main tree's folder by path. Verified with a PATH shim that makes `ln` fail: `worktree-add` succeeds, the dependency folder is a real copy, shared state is read from the main tree. Why: a run started in a worktree wrote its own `ACTIVE_RUN` while the hook read the main tree's, so the hook saw no run (the implementer's window never opened and its writes were judged as in no run); `node_modules` linked to the main tree let `npm install` in a task change the main tree; untracked `.env` files were missing from a worktree; and links break on Windows. Rejected: one `ACTIVE_RUN` in the main tree for every run (two runs would fight over one selector); keeping the links with a fallback (a link that is a copy goes stale without anyone noticing); read-only sharing of dependencies with copy-on-change (needs a file system overlay that is not portable); installing dependencies in each worktree automatically (network, and `safety.dependency_changes_require_task_authorization`); copying a `.env` git does not ignore (a `git add -A` would commit it). Amended in review: the build-record export now COPIES the dependency folders named by `worktree_deps` (`worktree-prep.sh --deps`) instead of linking `node_modules`, `vendor` and `.venv` from the project (a build or install step could write through the link); `worktree-prep.sh` also re-points a relative link that leaves a copied folder and resolves into the main tree, and reads its prune list from the data only (no hardcoded folder name). The shared "Isolated execution" rule of the skills now says an evidence worktree links dependency folders only while no step installs or changes packages (otherwise it copies them), and that a proofline run worktree always gets copies. Amended in round 2: the prompt hook also approves the pending run-bound requests (scope, waive:*, destructive, single_step, budget, reopen) of runs that live in a worktree: a glob of the main tree's worktree folders finds a pending request without starting a process, `agent.sh worktree-root` must confirm the folder as a registered worktree, and that worktree's `agent.sh approve-pending <ID>` runs under the same time budget; the approval log is the one shared `approve.log` of the main tree; `safe_state_file` accepts a capture or request under the main tree's shared folders (its walk ended at the worktree root, which refused every capture approval made from a worktree). A failed build-record says that the clean export holds no git-ignored file such as `.env` (secrets are never copied into it), and the batch `wait` line says that the owner pid is another live session. Round 6: the prompt hook runs a worktree's `agent.sh` only when it is byte-identical to the main tree's (a task could rewrite the tracked file); with several runs waiting, an approval reply binds to the run it names (else the hook asks which); `safe_state_file` accepts outside its own root only the shared folders and registered worktrees; `approve.log` is rotated under a lock.
- **A186. 0.0.33, a CI-fix round on every platform and the platform from config (amends A160, A180).** What: (1) *Failed-log adapter.* A180 left CI-fix rounds on GitHub only, because the failed-log reader was `gh run view --log-failed` inside `agent.sh`. The reader moves into the platform adapter: `platform.sh ci-failed PR SHA --cli PATH` prints one failed check as `RED<TAB>id<TAB>name<TAB>status<TAB>read|none`, a `LOG` line and the log text. GitHub reads the failed workflow run (`gh run list`, `gh run view --log-failed`, `gh pr checks`), GitLab the head pipeline of the merge request (`glab mr view`, the failed job through `glab api`, its log through `glab ci trace`), Azure DevOps the rejected or broken build policy (`az repos pr policy list`) and the error messages the build timeline recorded for the failed tasks. `agent.sh` keeps the common round (record, amend, fix, commit, push, at most two attempts), strips control characters and keeps the last 80 lines; it contains no platform command. When the tool cannot give the log (an error, an empty answer) the adapter answers `none` with the name and status, and the round starts from those two alone: the log file, the round's output (`NOTE: ...`) and the fix instruction say so. Bitbucket, other hosts and a missing tool have no reader at all, so no failed check is known and `ci-fix` refuses with a message that names the platform and the tool; it never invents a red check. (2) *Platform from config.* `git.platform` (github|gitlab|azure|bitbucket|other) and `git.platform_host` (a bare host such as gitlab.company.com) name a private host. Precedence: config, then `PROOFLINE_PLATFORM`, then the origin URL; `platform.sh detect` prints `source: config|env|auto` and `proofline doctor` shows it. `platform_host`, when set, applies `git.platform` only when it equals the host of the origin URL as a whole (case-insensitive equality, never a prefix, suffix or substring), so `github.com.evil.example` stays `other` and a configured platform is not carried to another host; the auto-detected hosts are unchanged. Adapters follow the host: `platform.sh env` gives `GH_HOST` (GitHub Enterprise) or `GITLAB_HOST` (self-hosted GitLab), exported by `agent.sh`, `proofline merge` and `batch.sh` before they call the tool; an Azure DevOps Server origin (`host/<collection>/<project>/_git/<repo>`) yields an organization URL passed as `--org`. `config-check` validates the two keys (a platform from the list, a bare host name, no host without a platform). Why: private GitLab and Azure users could deliver but not have a red CI fixed, and a self-hosted host needed an environment variable on every machine. Rejected: matching `platform_host` by suffix (it would admit `evil-gitlab.company.com.attacker.example`); a `--no-log` override (the round must say what it did not see); guessing a check name when nothing is readable (a made-up red would open a fix round for nothing). Residuals: the glab and az output shapes follow their documented JSON and were exercised only against fake tools here, not a real GitLab or Azure DevOps; the Azure reader returns task error messages, not the raw task log; `az` and `glab` have no read of a check that is not tied to a merge request pipeline or a build policy. Amended in review: `git.platform` without `git.platform_host` applies to any origin, so when the origin host is not an exact known host of that platform `agent.sh config-check` and `proofline doctor` WARN (`platform.sh warn`, `agent.sh platform-warn`) and `platform.sh env` exports no `GH_HOST` or `GITLAB_HOST` for it.
- **A187. 0.0.33, workspace commands are built from the member list in data, and no shared script branches on an ecosystem name (related A173, A174, A176).** What: (1) `workspace_roots[].members` in `ecosystems.json` states which file lists the members and how it is parsed (`single_prefix`, `block_open`, `block_close`, `block_item_prefix`, `comment`, `format`); a command rule with `workspace` and `at_workspace` is the template, `{members}` the list. `discover.sh` (`d_members`, `d_rule`) reads that and produces the command; a workspace rule comes first and applies only when the list is not empty and every member is a safe path. First user: Go, `go.work` (`use` lines and `use ( ... )` blocks) gives `go build ./svc/api/... ./svc/worker/...`, `go test` and `go vet` the same way, with `go -C <dir>` for a nested workspace. A `go.work` without a root `go.mod` used to give nothing (and `init` named Go as ambiguous); with a `go.mod` it ran `go build ./...`, which builds only the root module. `ecosystems.mjs validate` checks the new data (format holds `{member}`, a parse mode exists, the patterns are regular expressions, a workspace template needs `{members}` and a `members` entry). Moved: none of the other ecosystems. Cargo, npm/pnpm/yarn/bun, uv, Maven, Gradle and Dart already express a workspace as `workspace_roots` plus an ordinary bare command; their tool runs the whole workspace from the root, so a member list would only change the command (`cargo test --workspace`, `pnpm -r`), which A187 does not do. .NET has no workspace file; the solution file is its target. (2) A static rule in `tests/shared/check-static.sh` (rule 5, also in CI's static job) fails when a line of a shared shell script (`bin/`, `control-plane/agents/`, `adapters/`, `skills/*/scripts`; not `platform.sh`, `ecosystems.sh`, the self-tests or comments) has a case arm or a comparison naming an ecosystem id; the ids are read from `ecosystems.tsv`. Violations found and fixed: `doctor.sh` chose `major.minor` for `go|python` (the default is now `major`; `runtime.compare` already says how many components), `run-bench.sh` listed the runtimes and branched on `go` and `java` to print versions (it now reads `runtime.name` and `runtime.local.commands` from a skill-local copy of the definition, `tool_version.<runtime.name>`, so `python3` and `rustc` are keyed `python` and `rust`), and the process-group method `python` in `discover.sh` is renamed `pysetpgid` (it names a launcher, not an ecosystem). Interpreter names in the Claude runtime hook (`python`, `ruby`, `php`) are the interpreters whose inline code the process guard reads; they carry `# eco-ok: <why>` on the line above, which the test accepts. Why: a script that knows "go" has to be edited for every new ecosystem, and the same knowledge drifted into three places. Rejected: a member list parser per ecosystem in sh (the knowledge again); moving the other workspace roots to member templates (changes behaviour, no gain); a fixed list of names in the test (it would drift from the definition). Known limits: the rule scans shell scripts and hooks only; the node probes (`impact.mjs` symbol analysis, `diff-manifests.mjs` manifest parsers) are language parsers and are not covered; an interpreter line needs the `eco-ok` marker; only the `use` shape of `go.work` is parsed (replace directives and `toolchain` lines are ignored, a quoted path is unquoted). Amended in review: the browser-test dependency probe of `agent.sh` (which package names, in which manifest, installed under which folder) is data, `browser_test` in `ecosystems.json`, and `check-static` rule 5 also fails a line of a shared shell script that names a plain manifest, project or lock file of an ecosystem (a line may be marked `# eco-ok:` with a reason).
- **A188. 0.0.33, fewer processes on the hook's hot paths, measured by counting (related A171, A185).** What: (1) *Measurement.* `tests/bench/hook-procs.sh` (not run by CI) puts a PATH shim in front of every external command the hook and the `agent.sh` it calls may run, starts each event in a throwaway installed project with `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` set as the runtime does, runs it once to warm up (first-run state such as the baseline is not counted) and reports the median of `REPEAT` runs (default 3): external executions and milliseconds. Shell builtins and command-substitution forks are not counted, so the count is a lower bound of what a Windows fork-emulating shell pays. There is no Windows machine here and no Windows runner existed in `ci.yml`; no Windows measurement was possible. The estimate is therefore arithmetic only: at an assumed 20 to 50 ms per process in Git Bash, a Bash PreToolUse of 101 processes cost roughly 2 to 5 s per tool call, recording an approval 10 to 25 s (against the 20 s step budget and the runtime's 30 s limit). A nightly and manual job `hook-time-windows` (windows-latest, Git Bash, A164 style; not in `checks`, `continue-on-error`) now runs the same script and writes the per-event table to the job summary, so the real numbers will exist after the first nightly run. (2) *Reduction, behaviour byte-identical.* One `jq` or `node` run reads every JSON value an event needs (`jprefetch`; it also validates the input, replacing the empty `jget`), and a later `jget` with the same path list is answered from memory; a value that holds the cache's separator characters or a NUL is not cached and falls back to the old process. `dirname`, `basename`, the ACTIVE_RUN read (`sed` and `tr`), `safe` for names that are already safe, the `-` to `_` role name, the SHA-256 digest word (`awk`), the JSON text escape (`awk` only when the text holds a backslash, quote, tab, CR or newline), the prompt capture (`cat`, `jesc`, `sed`, `cp` replaced by the value already in memory), the `.approving` housekeeping (`find` only when a marker exists), the `<task-notification>` test (`head`), the command normal form of the dispatch-marker check (`sed` only when the text has a quote, backslash or dollar), its `PROOFLINE`/`DISPATCH` and `.agents` glob greps, the last user prompt in the stop hook (`sed`, `sed`, `head`) and the friction `awk` (only when the message names `agent.sh`) became parameter expansion, `case` or builtin reads. The clock is taken once at the start (`hk_tick` sets milliseconds and seconds without a subshell; the kill guard's time budget, the lock stamp, the ledger line and the capture time reuse it; a `date` that lacks nanoseconds, as on macOS, switches to `perl` once instead of trying `date` on every tick), the in-flight marker is removed by the single `rm` of the exit trap, and `mkdir -p` runs only when the folder is missing. The three database lookups of one event (`db-config` plus three `sed` and three `head`), `config-get tasks.dir`, `config-get canonical_branch` and `config-get product.dir` are one `agent.sh hook-config` call per event (it prints the database settings and the three values; an agent.sh without it, or a role it refuses, falls back to the old calls); `hook-config` and `db-config` take no lock, because they only read the config, which is parsed before any lock; `config-get`, `db-config`, `hook-config`, `worktree-root` and `in-knowledge-scope` no longer read the ecosystem definition, which none of them uses; `agent.sh` finds its own folder by parameter expansion. The migration-command check of the database guard ran two processes for each of about seventeen patterns for every simple command in a Bash call (`sed` trim and `grep`); the patterns are split and trimmed once and matched by one `grep` with the whole newline-separated list (status 1: no match; status 2, an invalid pattern in the list: the per-pattern loop as before). The approval path of `agent.sh` normalised every allowed sentence and phrase with its own five-process pipeline (about 210 processes per approval); `approval_norm_lines` normalises them all in one pipeline (the whitespace squeeze leaves newlines alone, so each line is what `approval_norm` gives alone; checked against it on the sentence list and edge lines in `sh` and `dash`), the request sequence numbers use `seq3` (no `basename`, `cut`, `sed`), the digest helper has no `awk`, and the hook's wait for the approval step sleeps 0.1 s for the first second and 0.5 s afterwards (a `sleep` is a process; the budget is unchanged). (3) *Result* (external executions per event, median, before then after, counted with the same script on the commit before and on this change): PreToolUse Write by an implementer with a window 61 then 11, Read 42 then 9, Bash `git status` 101 then 33; PostToolUse 20 then 7; prompt without an approval 28 then 10; prompt that records an approval 500 then 206; stop 56 then 32; session start 165 then 138; subagent start 135 then 77; subagent stop 29 then 14 (each count includes the hook's own `sh`). Time on this loaded macOS machine fell in the same proportion (Write 480 ms to 160, Bash 750 to 280, approval 2.1 s to 1.4 s). Why: the hook runs on every tool call, so its process count, not its logic, is the cost that grows with the length of a session, and Git Bash on Windows is the platform where a process is slowest. Rejected: caching the config answers in a file between events (an invalidation rule on `config.yaml`, `agent.sh` and the ecosystem definition is a new way to be wrong, and an unchanged answer is cheap once it is one process); dropping the ledger flush of `hook-time` from the stop and prompt events (it is the largest remaining cost there, about twenty processes, but how often the lines reach the ledger is a behaviour the friction report counts on); a rewrite of the shell scanner and merge guard in one `awk` (the largest remaining part of a Bash call, about twenty processes; it would change what they see); removing the shim's blind spot by counting subshell forks (not measurable without a tracer on every platform). Residuals: the Bash path still starts about thirty processes (the merge guard, the shell scanner and the kill guard are grep and tr pipelines over the command text), session start and subagent start are about 140 and 80 (`next`, window open and the ledger writes of `agent.sh`), each ledger write is about eight processes (hash chain, lock, sequence), and `build-record.sh` still links `node_modules`, `vendor` and `.venv` into its export with symlinks (a Windows copy there is a separate change).
- **A189. 0.0.34, "never invent" covers facts only; in the product skills the agent proposes and the user decides.** What: the rule "never invent" in `product-discovery`, `product-assess` and `product-spec` is narrowed to FACTS ONLY (a number, a name, a quote, a date, what a competitor does): a fact carries its source or is marked unknown. Assumptions, risks, opportunities, competitors to look at, edge cases, alternatives and questions are no longer forbidden; the agent must bring them, and the user accepts, changes or rejects each one. Why: an independent review found that the model could not propose risks, assumptions or opportunities, so the pre-mortem only echoed the user; numbers banned in assumptions contradicted the thresholds `product-assess` asks for; the PRD skipped error states, permissions and other topics nobody mentioned. New: (1) a `[proposal: <type>]` marker (pending, an error in a finished file); the origin suffix `source agent accepted by user` or `changed by user` on assumptions and decisions; a `## Rejected proposals` ledger (`- RP-n <text> rejected by user: <reason>`, quoting the user's own words). (2) A minimum contribution the checkers count, accepted or rejected: 5 agent items in the pre-mortem, 5 in the assumptions, 3 never-mentioned topics in the spec review (`check-review.mjs`, part of `--ready`). (3) A number in an assumption needs `estimate "<basis>"`; a basis has at least 3 words and a digit, an id (C-n, INT-n, AS-n) or a source or unit word; digits glued to letters (OAuth2, S3) are not numbers. (4) Discovery: a research method (search plan, "searched, not found", critical facts with an independent second source, stale web facts), competitor profiles with implications for us, 3 to 7 insights with "so what" (`check-insights.mjs`), a reasoned opportunity ranking. (5) Spec: a PRD completeness list (ten topics, one line each, `check-prd`); the review is checked against the same list. (6) A quality rubric (five questions) and a shallow and a good example per skill; up to three questions per message with lettered options. (7) `ASSUMPTIONS.md` holds sourced facts (`- C-n <text> [fact: ...]` under `## Facts`), and `product-assess` proposes a FRAME update through `product-discovery` when an assessment settles a FRAME unknown (it never edits `FRAME.md`); risk responses must not contradict each other (judged item). (8) Migration: product files written before 0.0.34 fail the new checks until updated; nothing rewrites them, and `docs/concepts/product.md` lists what each file needs. Rejected: scores for quality (a number invites gaming; the rubric stays a judged list); checking user acceptance in the checker (a checker reads text and cannot tell that the user, not the agent, wrote "accepted by user"; the skill asks and quotes the answer, review judges it); a waiver line for the minimum (rejected proposals already count, so the user is never blocked); a script check for conflicting `response:` fields (a negation heuristic gives false positives). Real-session evidence: the product skills ran in real sessions with web tools (competitors for the plugin itself; a sample menu site: frame, assumptions, pre-mortem) and passed the rubric. No model is called in the tests; the behaviour of the prose is judged by review.
- **A190. 0.0.34, `verification.env_files`: secret-free test env files in the build record's clean copy.** What: the build record's export still holds no git-ignored file, so no `.env*`. The config list `verification.env_files` (space-separated project-relative names, default empty, for example `.env.test`) names test env files that may enter it. Each listed file is scanned first with `secret-scan.sh` (unquoted `KEY=value` lines included); one visible secret rejects the run with exit 2, naming the file and line, never the value. `config-check` validates the key (no leading `/`, no `..`, no glob). Why: a project whose tests need `.env.test` could not pass its build record, and copying every `.env*` would put secrets into a record. Constraint: the built-in scanner reports every `KEY=value` of an env file as `env_file`, so the listed files are scanned as normalized copies; a project `commands.secret_scan` on those copies was checked for path shape only. Rejected: allowing every `.env*` (a secret reaches the record); a glob (a file nobody listed gets in). Real-session evidence: the 0.0.33 paths were exercised in one real batch of two trivial tasks, both merged to a local bare origin; `.env` stayed out and `.env.test` was in the build record. The missing-copied-files-list refusal (A169) and the doc-only knowledge exclusion (A184) paths were NOT exercised in a session, only by self-tests. Limits (round-1 review): the listed files are scanned by the token patterns and the quoted-value rule only; the `.env` rule does not apply to the normalized copies, so a low-entropy value such as `DB_PASSWORD=hunter2` passes and only secret-free files belong in the list; a `proofline:allow-secret` marker skips a line. A listed file whose parent directory resolves (symbolic links followed) outside the project or under `.git`, or that is itself a symbolic link, rejects the run; a listed file that does not exist only prints a note.
- **A191. 0.0.34, cleanup reads the last ledger line that is not a hook line (related A169).** What: `cleanup` required the last ledger line to be the terminate or knowledge-done event, but `hook-time` appends `event=hook` and `event=hook-timeout` lines after it, so a BLOCKED run was refused with "requires its ledgered terminate transition". It now reads the last line that is not a hook line. Why: found in a real session; no other reader takes the last ledger line as an event, and `ledger_append` still uses the real last line for the hash chain. Tested in `lifecycle-test.sh`.
- **A192. 0.0.34, the README is trimmed by about 10 percent and its bounds are lowered (related A153).** What: README 12500 to 11219 bytes and 154 to 144 lines; the UI craft detail, the ecosystem-skills note and the visual git client note moved to `design-surfaces`, `ecosystems` and `enforcement-layers`, the wiki note to the daily-use guide. The bounds in `check-static.sh` drop to 158 lines and 12340 bytes (slimmed size plus about 10 percent), which leaves room for a few lines about the product skills. Why: the README says what proofline is and how to use it; detail belongs in `docs/concepts`. Rejected: keeping the old bounds (the README would grow back unnoticed).
- **A193. 0.0.35, the Skill tool is redirected to the file, and a request for an internal command is sent back (amends A171).** What: (1) every proofline skill is `disable-model-invocation: true`, so a lead that calls one through the Skill tool starts nothing (seen in real use: `proofline-lead` never started a batch). The PreToolUse hook now matches `Skill` and denies a call whose target is a proofline skill (`proofline:<name>`, or an unprefixed name found in the plugin's `skills/` or the project's `.agents/skills/` that no skill of the user's own bears) with one line, "do not use the Skill tool; read <path>/SKILL.md and continue with the same step"; it applies to the lead and to subagents, and other skills are not touched. The entry skill, the lead (hard rule 15) and every role file (all generated agent files, Claude and Codex) say never to call a proofline skill through the Skill tool. (2) The Stop hook no longer only notes a message that asks the user to run `agent.sh`, `approve`, `answer`, `--no-verify` or to edit a file under `.agents/` by hand (also a line that starts with `!`, and a fenced command announced by such a request): it sends the message back once ("Do not make the user do this: do it yourself through the right path, or report it in one line as a proofline bug and write it to the friction report"), records the friction note, and on the retry (`stop_hook_active`) falls back to the A171 one-line message so the turn ends. `git push`, `gh auth login` and a plugin update are the user's own work and never match. Why: both were repeating failures in real sessions, and a note after the fact does not change the turn. Found while running the smoke test (A195) against Claude Code 2.1.312: the runtime rejects a Skill call for a `disable-model-invocation` skill itself ("cannot be used with Skill tool ... Ask the user to run /proofline:proofline-lead") before any hook runs; PreToolUse, PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure did not fire in a real session. The PreToolUse redirect therefore stays as a no-cost guard for versions that run hooks first, and the working parts are: the SessionStart context names the file and forbids the Skill tool, the entry skill, the lead and every role say so, and the Stop hook sends back (once) a message that gives up at that error or asks the user to run `/proofline:proofline-<skill>`, naming the file to read. Rejected: removing `disable-model-invocation` (the flag is what keeps 29 skills out of the model's own initiative); blocking without the retry guard (a loop when the model cannot comply).
- **A194. 0.0.35, plugin and install version skew is reported, and optional tools are used when present (related A153).** What: (1) `proofline doctor` and the SessionStart hook compare the plugin's version with `proofline_version` in the project's `.agents/config.yaml`; a difference is one WARN or one `systemMessage` line with the next step (`/proofline upgrade` when the project is older, a plugin update when it is newer), and the lead says it before it starts a run. (2) `doctor` shows `ast-grep` and `rtk` on one `tools:` line. proofline installs neither and requires neither. When `ast-grep` is installed, explorers and reviewers prefer it for structural searches (every use of a symbol, every instance of a finding class); otherwise `rg`/`grep`. (3) rtk's compression never touches evidence. rtk documents `RTK_DISABLED=1 <command>` as the per-command switch (its configuration guide; `rtk bypass <cmd>` also exists) and `hooks.exclude_commands` for permanent exclusions of command names, which cannot tell `git diff` in a review from `git diff` while exploring, so the per-command prefix is used. `agent.sh` and `build-record.sh` export `RTK_DISABLED=1` to everything they start.
